text: Index polynomials for chiral spinors, gravitini and self-dual forms, followed by anomaly descent, determine anomalous phases and counterterms with suitable modular transformations.

Act with Lie derivatives and exponentiated translations on a position-dependent metric family. Use Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff manipulations, a gravitational inverse Higgs relation, and projection onto localized modes to extract nonlinear transformations.

Solve the transverse-traceless linearized Einstein equation using the Lichnerowicz operator. Construct metric zero modes from Hessians of harmonic functions and assess localization with the metric L2 inner product.

Generate a finite-electric-field, back-reacted radial solution using string dualities. Evaluate its tensor equation and an Einstein-equation component, with computer algebra, to constrain the electric field and deformation parameter.

Scalar stationary conditions and second-derivative mass matrices identify the axion and CP-even inflaton candidate. A block neutrino mass matrix is treated in the hierarchical type-I seesaw approximation.

A Coleman-Weinberg one-loop potential feeds slow-roll observables and the e-fold integral. The curvature-perturbation amplitude fixes the quartic coupling; an effective two-scalar decay width estimates reheating.

Literature-based assessment using the relation between QFT and particular models as an analogy for string theory and its scenarios. The essay separates generic statements, construction-dependent predictions and observational challenges rather than presenting a new derivation.

Reviewed tools include dimensional reduction, effective field theory, geometry, branes, quantized fluxes, perturbative corrections and nonperturbative superpotentials. Phenomenological comparisons concern superparticle spectra, inflationary observables and post-inflationary cosmology.

Reconstruct Mellin poles and residues by matching logarithms to conformal blocks and Mack polynomials. Extract finite-spin anomalous dimensions using contour integrals, Hurwitz zeta functions, exponential regulators, and integral representations of polygamma functions.

Use the collinear Casimir with eigenvalue J²=(ℓ+Δ)(ℓ+Δ−1) to turn singularity matching into algebraic recursion in inverse J². For integer Δ, alternating-word harmonic polylogarithms construct the basis; selected examples admit finite-spin resummations.

Expand conformal partial waves through order 1/N4. The coefficient of log²u, proportional to a(0)(γ(1))²/8, supplies a known source; crossing maps it to an enhanced log²v singularity that constrains second-order OPE data.

Insert the resulting Jordan-frame expansion rate into the Boltzmann equation for Y = nχ/s̃ and x = mχ/T̃. For masses 5–1000 GeV, tune the annihilation cross section to Ω₀ = 0.27, the abundance target adopted in this historical analysis.

Numerically solve the conformal scalar master equation, or the coupled scalar–Einstein-frame Hubble equations for disformal coupling. Incorporate departures from radiation's equation of state using a Standard Model particle-threshold kick function.

Expand on-shell quantities in a deformation parameter λ and use the equations of motion together with off-shell no-scale contraction identities. Project the canonically normalized mass matrix onto real combinations of Ψ=T_I ΦI, with T_I=(Km,Ya), Ya=O(λ), including phase-rotated combinations when third superpotential derivatives contribute.

Choose Ya by solving linear equations that cancel a nonnegative square in the projected mass. Their invertibility follows from stabilization of all perpendicular moduli at the Minkowski point. A negative projected quadratic form establishes a negative eigenvalue even when Ψ is not a mass eigenmode.

Expose AdS factors through radial coordinate changes and warp-factor matching. For IIB AdS₆, a formal T-dual construction reduces the problem to one Toda-like equation; identification with the cited general IIB solutions is anticipated rather than demonstrated.

Choose local coordinates using closed or integrable vielbein combinations, then impose RR Bianchi identities away from sources to obtain additional PDEs. Separation of variables and further ansätze produce tractable examples.

Use the imported pure-spinor supersymmetry formalism, decompose six-dimensional bispinors over S² and M₄, and exploit spinor bilinears defining an identity structure to determine a local vielbein and fluxes.

Products of step functions vanish exactly when their induced time ordering contains a directed loop. The proof relates these loops to polarized energy poles, then uses polynomial continuation to obtain an identity for arbitrary abstract polar numbers.

Construct an energy-conserving orientation and loop-energy basis. For a connected graph, L=I−V+1; Proposition 1 assigns each basis energy to an oriented minimal loop and expresses internal energies with coefficients 0 or 1.

The proof temporarily represents polar numbers by rational functions of auxiliary energies, integrates loop energies and Fourier transforms. Pairwise cancellation at the lowest-time vertex establishes a coordinate-space identity; independence of exponential factors isolates surviving monomials.

Use maximally symmetric simplex momentum configurations to reduce external momentum dependence to one scalar p. Bilocal evaluations at p²=0,k² determine gravitational couplings; trilocal evaluations at 0,k²/2,k² separate p² and p⁴ contributions and test the R² contribution.

Find roots of the truncated beta functions and vary higher-vertex identifications to assess stability. Compare stability matrices obtained by identifying higher couplings before differentiation versus after differentiation; agreement of their most relevant eigenvalues is used as a convergence diagnostic.

Differentiate the effective-action FRG equation to obtain coupled propagator and vertex flows through four gravitons. Project external graviton legs onto transverse-traceless modes and Einstein–Hilbert tensor structures; retain higher-curvature information through momentum-dependent vertex dressings.

Embedding tensors contracted with scalar coset representatives organize masses and charges. Tensor gauge transformations remove redundant vectors from the democratic vector/tensor formulation, isolating propagating fields before expansion around a vacuum.

Compare two evaluations of large gauge transformations on Chern–Simons couplings; convert representation-weight sums into anomaly trace factors. In the geometric description, match these couplings to divisor intersections and flux pairings.

Integrate out massive parity-violating modes to obtain one-loop Chern–Simons terms. Infinite Kaluza–Klein sums are evaluated using the stated zeta-function regularization, including ζ(−1)=−1/12 and ζ(−3)=1/120.

Adapt tabulated dark-matter-decay deposition efficiencies because PBH energy injection is linear in density. Construct species-weighted PBH efficiencies for hydrogen ionization, Lyman-alpha excitation and heating, retaining energy and redshift dependence rather than instantaneous deposition.

Modify CAMB and HYREC with PBH mass and abundance parameters, evolve the recombination history and CMB spectra, and fit with COSMOMC. Main abundance limits use fixed base cosmological parameters and the paper's stated cumulative 95% confidence construction around the median.

Compute the redshift-integrated PBH photon intensity using the stated Hawking spectrum in its high-energy limit, then match it to the COMPTEL EGB upper bound. The comparison assumes PBHs may account for 100% of the measured background.

Other explicit methods include autonomous-system critical points and linearized eigenvalues for background attractors, scalar perturbations in conformal Newtonian gauge, and radial reconstruction of the potential from metric functions.

Background reconstruction sets φ=t and y=a^(3/2), reducing the potential model to a linear ODE with reconstruction V(t)=4ÿ/(3y). Related Riccati equations are linearized by a Sturm–Liouville substitution.
Plasma delay is obtained by integrating the free-electron contribution along the line of sight: ΔtDM=∫(dl/c)νp²/(2ν²). The observational normalization is ΔtDM=415 s ×(ν/1 GHz)⁻²×DM/(10⁵ pc cm⁻³).

Subtract modeled Milky Way and IGM dispersion from the observed total, then allocate the allowed residual to photon mass. The residual uncertainty combines measurement, Galactic modeling, cosmological-parameter and IGM-inhomogeneity uncertainties in quadrature; the mass-to-DM conversion also includes cosmological and redshift uncertainties.

Write Eexp(z)=√[ΩΛ+Ωm(1+z)³]. The IGM kernel is He(z)=∫₀ᶻ(1+z′)dz′/Eexp(z′), whereas the photon-mass kernel is Hγ(z)=∫₀ᶻdz′/[(1+z′)²Eexp(z′)]. The mass-induced differential delay is mγ²Hγ(z)(E1⁻²−E2⁻²)/(2H0) in the stated natural units.

A γ⁰-dependent phase rotation replaces the signed sound-speed coefficient by its magnitude and introduces effective-mass spikes. Nonadiabaticity estimates reproduce a finite momentum cutoff for nonzero gΦ. Perturbative inflaton decay and production from oscillating φ²-dependent masses are also estimated.

Use canonically normalized gravitino Lagrangians, Fourier/helicity decomposition, and the longitudinal mode equation. An analytic solution in the constant-g, vanishing-gravitino-mass limit determines Bogoliubov switching and occupation numbers; a momentum cutoff regulates the density integrals.

Approximate the Lorentzian propagator by complex solutions of the Euclidean field equations with specified real boundary configurations. Numerical shooting tunes the complex scalar data and complex-time contour; transition weights satisfy ptrans ∝ |T|².

Estimate action-gradient WKB ratios using finite differences between neighboring interpolating instantons. Asymmetric inflationary solutions are obtained by smoothly deforming the symmetric contour without crossing singularities.
Apply Schwinger–Zwanziger quantization to fractional charges, then track both charge and self-statistics of dyons under axion-angle shifts. This supplies a second argument for the proposed period.
Rescale Ã=A/t, g̃=g/t and θ̃=t²θ to an integer-charge theory, apply standard modular transformations, and pull them back using τ̃=t²τ.

Use quadratic BF-field elimination for bulk response. For the αbFTI surface example, use a projective parton construction, dyon condensation, surface pairing, and vortex statistics modulo transparent bulk particles.

Dimensionally reduce the exterior geometry to a radion cosmology with an axion-flux potential proportional to R⁻⁴. Analyze null trajectories in the candidate metric and apply the imported topological censorship theorem conditionally to loops.

Estimate topological inflation by comparing core size with Hubble radius, and independently compare coordinate-boundary collapse with proper metric expansion using a linearized flat-space scalar equation.

Numerically evolve axisymmetric Einstein–scalar equations from a flat-space string profile and Minkowski metric. Separately evolve Einstein–radion equations for a sample Wilson-loop model and fit the proper core expansion.

The surveyed analyses construct foliation-invariant operators, study linear perturbations and dispersion relations, count constraints using Hamiltonian methods, and calculate post-Newtonian parameters for specified matter couplings.

Renormalization arguments reviewed include stochastic quantization under detailed balance and a gauge ensuring regular anisotropic propagators, local relevant/marginal counterterms, and background-covariant treatment of gauge invariance.
Other methods include Stückelberg covariantization of the preferred foliation, Hamilton–Jacobi tunneling and ray tracing near horizons, and canonical Dirac quantization in 1+1 dimensions.

Analyze the imported Cohen–Kaplan exterior using the Kretschmann scalar and circumference derivative φ=dC/dr, then assess matching to a smooth core. Review imported Gregory solutions with a dynamical metric but static field profile.

Estimate magnetic-brane tension from field energy and compare core radius with Schwarzschild radius to motivate cutoff bounds. Extrapolating this dimensional argument to axions is explicitly treated as a naive singular limit.

Approximate the composite string by a radial continuum charge distribution. Balance string repulsion against domain-wall attraction, estimate its radius and field energy, and add the massive-axion wall profile's contribution.

Matches degeneration limits to effective-field-theory sunset and double-bubble diagrams. Mixed-sector integrals use Schwinger parameters, regulators, Poisson resummation and real analytic Eisenstein series; Prym periods and Schottky relations support suppression of non-level-matched contributions.

Uses the established gauge-fixed genus-two superstring formalism: split gauge, supermoduli integration, theta functions and modular forms, factorized GSO coefficients, and Poisson-resummed Narain lattices. A q-expansion extracts the leading untwisted contribution.

Semiclassical false-vacuum decay is described by Γ/Vol≈A exp(−B), with B the Euclidean bounce action minus the starting-state action. The authors include Einstein gravity and impose an O(4)-symmetric radial ansatz to estimate gravitational effects.

The thin-wall treatment separates exterior, wall and interior contributions. The sinusoidal wall is evaluated through a one-dimensional instanton, ψ±=4 arctan exp[±λ²(ζ−ζ0)], allowing its tension and thickness to be calculated rather than supplied as UV inputs.

Finite-time S-matrix amplitudes describe interactions of background constituents with external particles. The semiclassical subset keeps the background state unchanged. Particle-production rates use coherent-state overlaps and phase space; thermal-like high-energy suppression is estimated using cited multigraviton amplitudes and Stirling counting.

The authors construct a coherent state in a Minkowski Fock space whose field expectation value reproduces the approximate metric. Matching classical and constituent energy densities fixes the effective frequency, while occupation-number counting and gravitational coupling estimates determine N and α.

Science objectives are translated into observational thresholds and mission requirements using frequency-domain SNR estimates, instrument-noise transfer functions, sky/polarisation-averaged GW response, and Fisher Information Matrix parameter forecasts.

Local test-mass-to-bench and inter-spacecraft measurements are combined on the ground. Time-Delay Interferometry synthesizes virtual equal-arm interferometers to remove otherwise dominant laser-frequency noise; auxiliary laser modulation supplies ranging information.

Internal Einstein equations are contracted using N=h^{mn}∂/∂h^{mn} and metric-homogeneous potential classes NVn=nVn. Without metric derivatives in V, the stated constraint is c=−χ^{1/2}(N−1)(N−3)V/3. Higher-derivative terms require an additional functional-variation contribution.

The four-dimensional effective action supplies equations for A, β and βQ, supplemented by an internal constraint. Solutions use the matter-free vacuum ansatz A=e^{Ht}, H²=λ/3, and present-epoch expansions for the internal factors.

Dimensional reduction and constraints on time-dependent prefactors produce a nominally time-independent internal action and ξ equation. The chosen normalizations include α⁴=σγ and α⁴ΓR/(β⁴σ)=1, with η=β²/γ for the three-form prefactor.

Analytical treatment rescales the radial field by its time-dependent minimum and uses z=ln(m_inf t). The n=4 phase equation is reduced to an elliptic-function problem after freezing the radial field; n=6 is linearized near a radial fixed point and phase minimum.

Illustrative coupled-field numerical integrations are compared with asymptotic estimates and reheating yields. During inflation, a slow-roll axion background and a phase equation on the radial-minimum hypersurface estimate the initial angular velocity. The appendix constructs a supergravity potential using Kähler and superpotential couplings.

Use a general parametric apparent-horizon surface because a single-valued radial graph fails late in the evolution. Solve the expansion and parameter-gauge equations as an elliptic system using Newton line search; projecting out pure gauge corrections improves robustness.

Diagnose horizon geometry using embeddings and a normalized spacetime Kretschmann invariant. Estimate ring mass and angular momentum using apparent-horizon Komar integrals, with the mass estimate reliable only sufficiently near a steady state.

Solve the symmetry-reduced Einstein equations using the modified cartoon method, CCZ4 constraint damping, fourth-order finite differences and RK4 in GRChombo, with adaptive mesh refinement reaching 22 levels.

Construct the inflaton potential from tree-level D- and F-term contributions plus the waterfall-multiplet one-loop logarithmic potential. Convert Jordan-frame potentials to the Einstein frame and use the canonically normalized inflaton in slow-roll observables.

Numerically solve slow-roll evolution and evaluate observables about 55 e-folds before inflation ends. Matching A_s = 2.1 × 10^−9 fixes Λ, equivalently the FI scale; the remaining parameter plane is constrained by tilt, perturbativity, vacuum stability and a stated sensitivity criterion.

Nonlinear supersymmetry cosets, differential nilpotency constraints and composite-superfield identities relate spinor, chiral scalar and analytic Goldstino realizations. Descendants reconstruct constrained scalar superfields from Goldstini and their auxiliary component.

Chiral and projective action principles provide alternative off-shell formulations. Component reduction in a Goldstino unitary gauge, followed by standard superconformal gauge fixing, extracts the cosmological contribution.

Constrained variations under local chiral rescalings of X generate the nonlinear equation eliminating its independent auxiliary component. The same method is extended to the curved action and to the new real N=1 multiplet.

For two axions, integrate out the heavy combination during inflation. Study post-inflationary energy transfer using normal modes and a truncated quartic-plus-mixing potential near the minimum, distinguishing resonant chaotic and adiabatic conversion behavior.

Numerically evolve coupled inflaton/radiation energy-density equations including perturbative decay, thermal blocking and photon or electroweak dissipation. Infer the surviving energy fraction and follow its later transition from quartic to quadratic oscillations.

Use slow-roll evolution with inflation ending at |η| = 1, CMB normalization and the spectral index. Numerically evolve the full inflationary potential while varying θ; two tilt-compatible branches correspond to negative or positive horizon-exit field values.

Evaluate the prescription labelled exact by the authors, P_R=κ²H²/(8π²ε), on the numerical background; compare it with the potential-based slow-roll spectrum and extract CMB spectral parameters and r.

Numerically integrate the homogeneous scalar and Friedmann equations, obtain ε=−Ḣ/H² and the remaining e-fold count, and compare these background solutions with the potential slow-roll approximation across parameter choices.

Estimate the PBH formation fraction using a Gaussian tail, map inflationary exit time to PBH mass, evolve abundances relative to radiation, include Hawking survival limits, and integrate over logarithmic mass intervals at equality.

Construct effective f(R) models from linearized running and a curvature-based cutoff, transform to the Einstein frame and use slow roll. Dilaton-gravity alternatives solve coupled flow equations for F, V and K or construct scale-independent dimensionless scaling solutions.

Apply RG improvement either to field equations or to the effective action. Cutoff identifications use cosmic time, Hubble scale, curvature invariants or temperature. Action improvement generates additional terms from spacetime derivatives of G(k(x)).

Review the background-field functional RG equation, projection onto an Einstein–Hilbert ansatz with a Litim regulator, linearization around fixed points, stability eigenvalues, and numerical integration of the beta functions.

Reduce the scalar equations for an SO(D)-invariant geometry to affine geodesic motion on the scalar manifold, with conserved norm c. Use the radial gravitational constraint and compare the required end-to-end scalar distance with the available timelike geodesic length.

Use a solvable Lie-algebra parametrization and a coset representative L, with M=LL† and metric −½Tr[dM dM⁻¹]. Identify commuting Peccei–Quinn shifts, rotate the associated generators, and locate totally geodesic axion–dilaton subcosets.

Determine the Euclidean scalar continuation holographically: a shift-symmetric scalar is Wick rotated when it couples to an exactly marginal pseudoscalar operator whose Euclidean coupling acquires i. The Zamolodchikov metric correspondingly changes sign through the two-point function's i² factor.

Factorizations of anticanonical sections, sequential blow-ups and curve-supported ADE singularities construct gauge sectors. Higgs/Coulomb branch dimension counts are compared with changes in compact G2 Betti numbers.
Imported building-block cohomology and orthogonal lattice gluing give b2(Y)=rk R+dim kL+dim kR and b3(Y)=b3(ZL)+b3(ZR)+dim kL+dim kR−rk R+23, where R=NL∩NR.
Kaluza–Klein reduction of eleven-dimensional supergravity uses harmonic forms, Lichnerowicz and fermionic zero modes, followed by a Weyl rescaling to four-dimensional Einstein frame.

Characteristic numerical evolution uses null geodesics angled by tan ψ=c/R, rather than boundary-normal characteristics, to cover an extremal horizon. Residual radial coordinate freedom keeps ξ=0 at an apparent horizon.

The implementation uses doubled Chebyshev domains, a standard grid of 30 radial-boundary and 40 bulk-direction points, fourth-order Runge–Kutta evolution, and filtering through interpolation to grids with two-thirds as many points.

Diagnostics include |F²|, v d|F²|/dv and its logarithmic derivative. Reported numerical checks compare two constraint-based evaluations of Vn at the boundary, vary resolution, and compare subcritical late-time stress tensors with previously computed stationary solutions.

A qualitative reduction of the exterior 2-form action to its radial zero mode gives S ∼ ∫dt (∂t b)²/(f² R). Wave-packet spreading then estimates the time over which localized b can be treated classically.

Parametric energy accounting compares the leftover flux energy E ∼ b²/(f² L³) with the available black-hole mass M(Rc) ∼ Rc MP². The flux radius L is taken either as Rc = 1/sqrt(σ) or as the distance reached during the remaining evaporation time.

Derivatives of the pole-subtracted amplitude are expressed through positive spectral moments I(q,p). Inequalities comparing successive moments control the alternating signs introduced by t derivatives, allowing recursive construction of positive combinations Y(2N,M).

Cauchy contour deformation, Schwarz reflection, and crossing symmetry produce fixed-t dispersion relations. The Froissart–Martin growth estimate permits two subtractions; explicit s-, u-, and t-channel poles are then removed.

The optical theorem and partial-wave unitarity constrain Im al. Nonnegative derivatives of Legendre polynomials at forward scattering, together with analyticity of Im A in t, supply positive spectral derivatives throughout 0 ≤ t < 4m².

Impose a periodic-scalar winding condition, reduce its kinetic term with the KK connection, and identify the induced covariant derivative. Treat changing the winding sector separately from varying continuous fields within one sector.

Deform an existing Euclidean pair-production configuration by a flat connection supported on its nontrivial topology. If the action and asymptotic data are unchanged, the original nonzero amplitude supplies the corresponding period-labelled states.
Differentiate an invariant one-form ansatz in an orthonormal frame, impose a chosen Hodge duality sign, and integrate the resulting radial equation. Asymptotic normalization gives F=r/(r+Nλ²).

Move to a dual frame with an explicit Chern–Simons term, reduce its selected internal components, and map back. The method requires the flux sectors generated by duality, including non-geometric ones.

Move to a duality frame where the relevant vector comes from B_2, reduce the known Chern-Simons interaction, and map its coefficient back to the original compactification data. Keep distinct the fields and normalizations in the two frames.

Reduce the period and its kinetic action together, then inspect wrapped charged configurations in the lower-dimensional theory. A formal instanton phase is insufficient unless backreaction, infrared convergence, and boundary conditions permit the configuration.

Evaluate the sourced Euclidean saddle and infer E[C] from the large-time Wilson-surface exponent. The method assumes negligible gravity, a dilute instanton gas, and a consistent normalization of the axion and insertion.
Introduce suitable flux on three T⁶ two-cycles to induce D4, D2, and D0 charges and produce a finite-horizon black hole. The displayed unfluxed metric provides the horizonless comparison.

Test a proposed symmetry on the full set of connected flux configurations rather than only on its asymptotic vacuum. A finite bubble with a shift-dependent interior is sufficient to invalidate the original constant shift as an exact symmetry.

Fatten an overlapping instanton pair and retain the internal gauge flux that survives cancellation. This is an off-shell bubble construction whose action and Bianchi completion must be supplied before treating it as a saddle.

Add a one-degree-higher connection, covariantize the lower potential's field strength, and dress charged operators on bounding chains. The construction removes an independent global period shift by including it in gauge redundancy.
Use Hodge decomposition and the ∂∂̄ lemma to separate harmonic and nonharmonic parts of c3 and express the metric correction through derivatives of a scalar. Tensor computations employ xAct/xTensor.

Solve corrected background equations, then combine reduction of the classical action on that background with reduction of eight-derivative terms on the leading Calabi–Yau geometry. The apparent quadratic scalar potential cancels between these contributions.
Apply integrations by parts, Bianchi and Schouten identities, Weyl rescalings, and perturbative higher-derivative field redefinitions to organize the reduced actions and identify simpler field bases.

An approximate WKB S-matrix, optical theorem, partial waves, and general n-to-n phase space provide amplitude bounds. Repeating the analysis with the modified dispersion relation changes mode normalization and phase space, yielding revised strong-coupling estimates.

For approximately linear dispersion, a time-coordinate rescaling by the sound speed and canonical normalization expose background-dependent interaction scales for operators ϕ^N ϕ̇^M (∂iϕ)^(2L). The smallest physical scale diagnoses perturbative strong coupling after redundancies are removed.

Sample classical inflationary trajectories by solving field equations and the homogeneous FLRW Friedmann equation. Apply single-field slow-roll observables only when transverse acceleration and nonadiabatic interactions are negligible.

Seek a lattice basis reduced in the L∞ norm; extended LLL supplies an approximate L2-reduced basis. Locate interior vacua quadratically and sample intersecting fundamental domains, using numerical minimization beyond the quadratic regime.
Introduce Lagrange multipliers enforcing R(φ−δ)=0, with R=(Q_RQ^−1 | −I). The matrix R^T(RR^T)^−1R projects onto the transverse space and measures lattice misalignment.

Candidate multicritical behavior is modeled with two real order parameters and a Ginzburg–Landau potential containing quadratic anisotropy and a dangerously irrelevant quartic anisotropy ν at the O(2) fixed point.

Background-field anomaly analysis uses a triangulated lattice, simplicial cochains, coboundaries and cup products. A continuum derivation embeds SU(N) into U(N), represents the discrete background by (B,C) with NB=dC, and tracks characteristic classes and quantized counterterms.

Dimensional reduction gives the SU(2) CP variation ΔS₃d=iπ∫Y A∪B. The mixed anomaly is represented by inflow iπ∫M a∪A∪B, where a gauges CP, A gauges the zero-form center, and B gauges the one-form center; M is auxiliary, distinct from X.

Compute χ(Y) as the degree of c(TY)∩[Y]. Obtain Chern classes using explicit ambient blowups, Aluffi’s complete-intersection blowup formula and adjunction; push successively through the blowups and then through the ambient projective bundle to B.

Jacobi’s partial-fraction identity expresses complete homogeneous symmetric polynomials as sums over the hypersurface classes of a blowup center. Together with Segre-class identities, linearity and the projection formula, this supplies the exceptional-divisor pushforward theorem.

Evaluate charges at infinity, impose falloffs, integrate the mass primitive, and choose a compatible reference. The fermionic application restricts variations to δa=0; integrability in that sector does not authorize changing the leading spinor coefficient.

Construct normals to the deformed surface and solve directly for a generator in the perturbed geometry. This preserves the boundary modular flow and surface-gravity normalization without fixing the surface through a gauge transformation.

Vary the full action before eliminating torsion, retain surface terms, combine derivative variations, and then impose algebraic torsion. The expanded printed spinor Lie derivative contains a visually confirmed apparent typo, so the reconstruction uses its scalar definition.

The proposed route inserts torsionful geometry into spinning-body dynamics, uses charges in effective-one-body descriptions, and develops first-order evolution for fermion matter. Matching, evolution, waveform generation, and detector comparison remain future work.

Extract action surface terms, construct the Noether current, separate on-shell constraints, and integrate the boundary variation. A boundary primitive produces a full charge only for an integrable choice of boundary conditions.

BFV gauge fixing imposes constant lapse. A lapse redefinition and q=a² make the chosen reduced action quadratic in q, permitting Gaussian integration over fluctuations with fixed endpoints and leaving one oscillatory lapse integral.

Construct the Wheeler–DeWitt Green function from Airy solutions. Match its coefficients to the lapse integral near the turning point and compare asymptotic expansions for classical, no-boundary and non-classical boundary data.

Complexify the lapse and use downward flows of h=Re(iS/ℏ); Im(iS/ℏ) stays constant along a flow. Decompose the original contour into thimbles Jσ with coefficients nσ=Int(D,Kσ), where Kσ are upward flows. Endpoint arc estimates justify the contour deformation in the model.

Experimentally discovered algebraic relations between g, h and ξ reduce the remaining system to an autonomous third-order equation for g, whose order can be lowered by one. The authors then integrate numerically; the relations' deeper origin is left open.

Construct a radial metric and symmetry-respecting four-form ansatz using the SU(3)-structure of squashed CP3. Solve the Maxwell sector and reduce the Einstein equations to radial equations for f, g, h and ξ; Bianchi identities make one Einstein equation redundant.

Start numerical integration from an analytic near-bubble Taylor expansion because the highest-derivative coefficient vanishes at the bubble. Tune the bubble-size parameter to remove the remaining asymptotic logarithmic BF mode, then evaluate the vacuum-subtracted on-shell action.

Apply the imported ’t Hooft mechanism through phase counting and gauge/global generator mixing. Green–Schwarz-induced mixing removes one pseudoscalar direction; repeated breaking of anomaly-free gauge factors is used to retain a global direction.

Analyze possible heavy tree mediators and invoke supersymmetric non-renormalization for loops when assigning effective-operator suppression scales. Sum electromagnetic and color anomaly contributions from the corrected spectra to obtain the axion–photon coefficient.

Use the listed charge spectra, anomalous-charge conservation, orbifold selection rules and twisted-sector multiplicities to construct Higgsino and fermion mass matrices in terms of singlet VEVs and coupling parameters.
Independent Palatini variations of w and e produce torsionlessness and the vacuum Einstein equation. A Legendre transform and covariant Poisson brackets then use (w,S) as phase-space variables.

Nakanishi–Kugo–Ojima quantization introduces auxiliary β, ghost and antighost fields, adding gauge-fixing and Faddeev–Popov terms. The paper identifies de Donder gauge with dS_ab=0; the auxiliary-field equation yields this condition in Landau gauge.

Reduce flux-induced masses into SU(3) singlet/triplet components. Address the additional internal-Dirac contribution through the dual non-Abelian anti-D3 theory and its lowest fuzzy-sphere harmonics, rather than solving the abelian modified Dirac equation explicitly.

Fix kappa symmetry and static gauge, derive compensating supersymmetry transformations, and make field redefinitions giving standard nonlinear transformations at the north pole. Expand the potential and transformation projector around the polarized minimum to identify corrections.

Obtain the bosonic and quadratic-fermion NS5 actions formally by S-dualizing D5 actions. At the throat tip, use the flux leg structure and Majorana–Weyl bilinear identities to isolate the fermion mass matrix.

Lift an initially flat direction with a subleading coupling, track the induced inflaton and spectator masses, and test whether reducing the coupling delays backreaction without destabilizing saxions or lowering the effective-theory cutoff.

Construct F-term potentials from Kähler potentials and flux superpotentials, solve for displaced saxion minima, compute the inflaton's proper distance, and compare flux dependence of string, KK and moduli masses.

Extract leading fractional responses, estimate their onset, and intersect that estimate with cutoff and stability restrictions. This abstraction preserves the distinction between a local expansion, a tunable parameter family, and a controlled global trajectory.

Use analytically solvable prototype vacua where available. For O2, impose hq1=qμ1, leaving the axionic direction orthogonal to hc+qρ massless; first stabilize heavy fields, scale their fluxes, then perturb by additional inflaton-stabilizing fluxes. Infer Θc perturbatively from the resulting heavy-modulus/inflaton mass hierarchy.

Define Lorentzian amplitudes by continuing a common external-energy multiplier u through the first quadrant to 1. Deform loop-energy contours around poles while fixing endpoints at ±i∞; spatial loop momenta remain real.

Use BV fields/antifields and Siegel gauge, then construct 1PI vertices by summing 1PI graphs. Tree graphs of the 1PI action reproduce full Green’s functions; shifted-background Ward identities use the corrected BRST operator.

Integrate world-sheet differential forms over sections specifying local coordinates and PCO positions. Plumbing fixture w1w2=exp(−s−iθ), s≥0, realizes propagators; BRST identities and Stokes’ theorem relate vertex boundaries to multilinear product identities.

Uses adiabatic subtraction for the non-interacting theory, transforms the stress tensor into FLRW coordinates, and isolates the finite state-dependent contribution. The near-center four-dimensional energy density receives an explicit calculation in Appendix B.

Relates FLRW and static-patch mode expansions using Klein–Gordon normalization and analyticity across the horizon. Four-dimensional radial modes involve hypergeometric functions; horizon matching produces entangled number states and a thermal reduced density matrix.

Provides an alternative horizon-thermodynamic argument using dU=T dS−P dV, S=A/(4G), and T=H/(2π). Changes in internal energy and volume refer to the hidden region, introducing minus signs relative to changes inside the Hubble sphere.

Conditions growth on a break, restricts to transitions whose precursors include the entire pre-break causet, and rearranges relative-probability binomial sums using the stated convolution identity. Bell causality then removes exterior spectators to treat a branching child universe.

Uses the imported CSG transition law P(C_n→C_{n+1})=λ(ϖ,m)/λ(n,0), where ϖ counts precursor elements and m counts its maximal elements. λ is defined through binomially weighted dynamical parameters; transition products determine finite growth-history probabilities.

The authors minimize superpotential F-terms, isolate symmetric and antisymmetric multiplets, and examine soft supersymmetry-breaking contributions. String examples use the N=1 supergravity potential, canonical normalization and a perturbative expansion of the corrected Kähler potential.

Instanton couplings are analyzed through Grassmann zero-mode integration. Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch gives the ED3–D7 index; a Koszul sequence, Serre duality and line-bundle cohomology supply an illustrative vector-like zero-mode example.

Symmetry-based effective operator analysis organizes a periodic axion potential using hidden-sector VEVs, Higgs bilinears and singlet powers. The hierarchy exponent is indexed by n=2k+m for visible factors s^(2m)(h†h)^(2k).

Massless-state combinatorics are compared with polynomial complex-structure deformations of weighted-projective Calabi–Yau hypersurfaces or complete intersections. Candidate geometries and Hodge numbers then supply parent supergravity spectra.

Super-Higgs multiplet decomposition tests allowed massless spectra. A stochastic search added up to four simultaneous simple currents across billions of models, stopping after no new structures appeared for a long interval.

Simple currents generate modular invariant partition functions from RCFT characters. Products of their matrices remain modular invariant, but ordering matters because the matrices need not commute and later twisted sectors can restore previously projected states.
Project the background-field Wetterich functional RG equation onto the retained operators. Functional traces are evaluated with heat-kernel coefficients and Mellin transforms.

Choose an applicable semiclassical entropy inequality, calculate the infrared entropy with fixed renormalized couplings, and test a controlled physical process. The authors propose that an unexplained violation signals an obstruction to ultraviolet completion.

Expand the factorized kernel, integrate spectral moments through special functions, and retain the terms producing logarithms in the proper-time integral. The printed Chebyshev series and its convergence range require correction before this can serve as a validated general procedure.

Solve the background spectral problem, sum or integrate normalized modes, and integrate the heat-kernel trace over ds/s. In this paper the method computes the charged scalar determinant with arbitrary electric-background insertions, while keeping gauge and metric fields external.

Set the initial quantum correction to zero, write r_+² = R² + h, expand the area term and the proposed scalar entropy, and impose nonnegative total entropy change. The cancellation of h is meaningful only for a regular linear response.

Tune b2 to zero in the specified Morrison–Park-type hypersurface, read the enhanced algebra and matter from the discriminant, and match a Higgs branching. Reject a simple ordinary-Higgs interpretation when the tuned geometry develops non-minimal loci.

Use integer combinations of singlet charges to define the full charge lattice, choose its dual abelian basis, and compare charges of equal non-abelian representations in that basis. The identification with a geometric normalization remains conditional.

Orthogonalize an integral section divisor against the geometric directions that must not contribute to an independent abelian gauge field, then evaluate the resulting divisor on fibral curves. Base terms can be discarded for these charges because their fibral intersections vanish.

Use fourfold periods of the holomorphic (4,0)-form and a moduli-independent intersection pairing to construct the complex-structure Kähler potential and flux superpotential. Both the cycle basis and chosen G4 fluxes are restricted to primary horizontal cohomology.

Insert previously obtained toric period and intersection data for Xc* into the effective couplings, retaining leading polynomial interactions. The period computation itself is imported from earlier work.
Analyze the no-scale F-term scalar potential for ΦI=(z,z1,S). The classical Kähler-sector cancellation removes the usual −3|W|² term, and the illustrative branch is obtained by solving FI=0.

Dualize a super-Weyl invariant action before fixing the compensator. Its kinetic potential obeys Ω(λZ,λ̄Z̄)=|λ|^(2/3)Ω and its superpotential has degree one; a degree-two prepotential simplifies the nonlinear component relations by zAGABC=0.

Promote superpotential coefficients to chiral superfields X_A and introduce real or complex-linear Lagrange-multiplier superfields. For constant G_AB, the multiplier equations make X_A constant (real r_A or complex c_A). For field-dependent G_AB with invertible M_AB=Im G_AB, they instead constrain M^{AB} Im X_B and yield X_A=e_A+G_AB(Φ)m^B, with constant real e_A,m^B; X_A generally remains field-dependent. Integrating out different fields yields either the original theory or constrained single/double three-form multiplets, including boundary terms.

For the IIA example, compute bosonic components, transform to Einstein frame, eliminate spectator auxiliary fields using their no-scale identity, and integrate the three-form equations to recover flux integration constants and the scalar potential.

In product targets, calculate open-string states using Floer cochains and Dolbeault resolutions of Ext groups, then construct a Chern–Simons-type string-field action. A noncommutative deformation of the B-model changes the differential and produces nonzero Chern–Simons level.

For partition functions, use radial quantization and local-operator BRST cohomology on S2×S1. On S3, expand matter determinants in characters and evaluate the supersymmetric matrix integral through Weyl sums and Gaussian integration, yielding WZW S and framing T factors.

Complete the gauge theory in BV–BRST form using inhomogeneous gauge and matter fields, ghosts, and antifields. The authors state that off-shell gauge invariance makes the resulting action satisfy the classical master equation.

Employ quantum-group representations, a regularized Verlinde formula, and analytic continuation to self-dual variables for state counting; use infinitesimal Wilson loops to regularize the singular boundary contribution.
Adapt an ADHM matrix parametrization to complex coordinates on CP¹×CP¹; introduce J=D₂ᵀD̄₁ and express self-duality through a differential constraint on J.

Use self-dual Ashtekar/Plebanski variables, the ansatz F=λΣ, and the Bianchi identity to extend the gauge construction to gravity; identify isolated-horizon boundary symplectic terms with Chern–Simons theory.

For E6 classification, balance the training classes and use logistic regression and factor analysis to reduce 76 inputs to two. Refine the resulting hypothesis using explicit toric monomial-survival inequalities.

Compare supervised algorithms using ten-fold cross-validation. For facet triangulations, train CART on point, interior-point, boundary-point, and vertex counts, then combine predicted facet counts into approximate polytope counts.
Fit gauge rank using leaf-height counts H₁,…,H₆. Interpret the linear decision function using integer ranks and geometric prior knowledge, obtaining the approximate expression 8H₁+4H₂+2H₃+H₄.

Construct continuous fluxes using the Hodge/period decomposition: choose a moduli-space point and ZiS, solve the Z eigenvector condition, set W0 accordingly, tune FI along that eigenvector, and finally minimize the full potential.

Expand the F-term potential and Hessian in inverse volume and small FI/W. Use the reviewed no-scale mass spectrum and matrix perturbation theory to estimate whether intersector mixing changes stability.

Impose radial-boost invariance and stress-tensor conservation, expand diagonal components in inverse powers of r, and infer their coefficients from the trace. Evaluate this source on the classical RN metric before integrating the first metric correction.

Derive temperature from the corrected horizon, use the first law for entropy and chemical potential, maximize black-hole-plus-radiation entropy for equilibrium, and apply thin-shell matching conditions to obtain an effective collapse potential.

Locate extremality through f=f′=0, using separate charge-dominated and small-charge expansions plus numerical solutions. Appendix A studies a sixth-degree horizon polynomial; Appendix B examines the nonuniform small-charge expansion.

Hierarchical scalar-potential analysis: supersymmetric D/F-term stabilisation at O(V^-2), α′, string-loop, single-instanton and matter contributions at O(V^-3), followed by poly-instanton stabilisation of cp at O(V^(-3-p)), p>0.

Order-by-order canonical normalisation in the inverse-volume expansion, followed by mass-matrix eigenvalue estimates and extraction of axion interaction scales. These are calculations reported by the authors, not reproduced here.

Euclidean continuation of the coupled scalar/Friedmann equations, with a short scalar bounce treated perturbatively on an approximately fixed geometry. A WKB estimate supplies the action difference between the Euclidean SHU with and without the scalar bounce.

ADM expansion, integration of the nondynamical lapse perturbation and a gauge-invariant scalar variable reduce the fluctuation problem to an effective Schrödinger equation. A numerical shooting method is used to investigate negative eigenmodes.

Uses covariant multi-field background equations, an orthonormal adiabatic–entropic decomposition, and ADM lapse/shift constraints to obtain the quadratic scalar action in spatially flat gauge; subsequently relates field fluctuations to gauge-invariant comoving curvature perturbations.

Compares analytic backgrounds with numerical evolution for exponential and quadratic potentials. Numerically evolves coupled Fourier modes in the leading de Sitter, constant-h approximation and fits their late-time enhancement relative to the h=0 test-field solution.

Continuous-wave NMR scans B0 until the Larmor frequency matches the unknown axion frequency. The transverse pseudo-field then builds transverse magnetization, whose precession produces the measured magnetic signal.

The nonresonant protocol applies a π/2 pulse, observes free precession, expands longitudinal frequency modulation in Bessel functions, and searches for sidebands. Clock-synchronized transients are averaged coherently within the ALP coherence time; independent sets are combined by averaging power spectra.

Construct deformations of Poincaré-invariant CFTs using primary operators of selected tensor type and dimension, then test explicit scalar examples through their stress tensors. For holography, exhibit an Einstein–Proca solution and discuss its type IIB embedding.

Use conformal Lie-algebra closure to classify allowed extensions. Analyze canonical/Noether stress tensors, conserved currents, and local improvement terms to determine when the special conformal current exists.

Specify the infrared spectrum, vary the compactification radii, and compare positive fermionic Casimir terms with negative photon and graviton terms. The source uses earlier potential calculations to decide whether the fermions intervene early enough and to bound their masses.

Substitute a valid mass-generation relation into a mass inequality and solve for the order parameter. Track fixed parameters explicitly: a quadratic seesaw map and a linear Dirac map produce different powers, and vanishing couplings can eliminate the constraint.

Reduce the two kinetic terms along a stabilized-volume constraint and canonically normalize the remaining direction. The appendix generalizes this fusion calculation to τ1 = cτ2^p, obtaining α̃1 = α1 + p⁻²α2 and α̃2 = α2 + p²α1; fibre inflation uses p = −2.

Construct effective supergravity through the Kähler function G and a nilpotent-field metric GSS̄ = m3/2²/(3m3/2² + V), with V = Λ + Vstab + Vinfl. Match stabilization locally near the volume minimum and analyze orthogonal masses using a small ε = m/M expansion.

Splits canonical energy into nonnegative gravitational/electromagnetic horizon fluxes and a late stationary contribution. The latter is evaluated using a comparison Kerr–Newman family with parameters affine in its family parameter, giving EΣ1=−κδ²A_B^KN/(8π).

Uses diffeomorphism-covariant Lagrangian identities, Noether charges, and the symplectic current. Canonical energy is EΣ=∫Σω(φ;δφ,Lξδφ), with ξ the background horizon Killing field. A second variation relates this quadratic quantity to second-order mass and angular-momentum changes.
Dimensional reduction to a three-dimensional Einstein frame, and strictly two-dimensional constraint and localized-fluctuation analyses using Breitenlohner–Freedman bounds.

One-loop functional determinants with a generally covariant path-integral measure; zeta-function analytic continuation, Poisson summation, and generalized Chowla–Selberg methods. The divergent vacuum-energy contribution is subtracted using the flat-space cosmological-constant counterterm.

Match a real Kähler potential and holomorphic superpotential to dimensionally reduced brane kinetic, mass and uplift terms, using modular covariance and nonlinear supersymmetry. The direct flux-background brane calculation is quadratic in fermions; remaining leading-order couplings are inferred through the supergravity completion.

For non-renormalisation, assign R-charges and promote flux/dilaton symmetry-breaking parameters to spurions. Write W = G0 w(ϕα, Gs/G0), with Gs including flux spurions and X. Rescale e^φ → λe^φ, G3 → λ⁻¹G3 and Θ → λ⁻¹/²Θ, giving an overall λ⁻² action and a reorganized loop-counting argument.

Complex-time representations of no-boundary saddle points relate inflationary histories to interior, locally Euclidean AdS domain walls. Euclidean AdS/CFT then supplies the large-three-volume holographic wave-function representation used in the analysis.

The free-theory Gaussian integral becomes a determinant of −∇² + m² + R/8. Analytic eigenvalues for a singly squashed sphere are combined with heat-kernel regularization: low-energy modes are summed numerically, while cutoff-dependent ultraviolet contributions are fitted to extract a finite part.

The critical O(N) partition function is obtained through an auxiliary-field integral transform of the free theory after a double-trace deformation. The critical limit is f → ∞; the source normalization is taken as ρ = 1, and the transform is evaluated by a large-N saddle approximation.

The analysis tracks cosmic energy density from CMB horizon exit to the present. The usual reheating matching equation receives an additional Nmod2/4 contribution from volume-modulus domination; reheating is represented by its duration Nre and an effective equation-of-state parameter wre.

The authors combine an approximate ns(N*) relation with e-fold matching, convert Nre to the last reheating temperature, and compare curves at fixed wre with historical Planck likelihood intervals. A least-squares fit summarizes the canonical-reheating temperature–tilt relation.
Combine trace-reversed Einstein equations with the five-form Bianchi identity and integrate over the compact space to constrain the vacuum energy through an on-shell potential.
Analyze four-dimensional uplift backreaction perturbatively and parametrize anti-brane interactions using S²=0 and W=W0+bS+A(1+cS)exp(iaρ); matching classical limits does not determine c.
Use classical ten-dimensional supergravity with a D7 fermion-bilinear source, solve for induced ISD/IASD fluxes, and evaluate their localized and bulk contributions with a string-scale cutoff.

Blinded spectra are fitted with multicomponent Voigt profiles using nonlinear χ² minimization. Models are trialled at Δα/α = 0 and selected by minimum reduced χ². After unblinding, velocity structure is held fixed in form; Δα/α is then freed while component parameters are reoptimized.

Solar-twin supercalibration compares approximately 500 km/s spectral chunks with a Fourier-transform solar reference. Linear velocity-shift trends are fitted separately for each detector chip. Direct comparisons of quasar exposures estimate slit shifts before corrected exposures are recombined.

Systematics are assessed by introducing distortion models, recombining exposures on eight nearby pixel dispersions, and refitting alternative absorption models. The intra-order test uses a saw-tooth velocity pattern of about 100 m/s; redispersion uncertainty is estimated from the resulting measurement scatter.

Evaluate the thermal weight branch by branch with fixed-charge boundary data. The operation produces a semiclassical contribution or comparison weight; it does not establish stability, dominance, or an exact finite-N partition function.

Resolve charge branches, impose |Q| at least one and the UV radius cutoff, then evaluate the dominant region of the resulting integral. Root expansions and endpoint prefactors require separate uniformity checks when g tends to zero.

Partition the trace by a conserved label, sum valid sector lower bounds, and compare with a benchmark. The abstraction does not equate ensembles or saddle sets; it requires positivity, nonoverlap, and uniform control of the selected sector weights.

Translate boundary current normalization into a bulk coupling using the Maxwell on-shell response to a boundary gauge source. Charge normalization must remain fixed; otherwise, rescaling the current can imitate a change in coupling.

At fixed energy, compare the entropy accumulated over charged sectors with that of a neutral small AdS black hole. This proposed ensemble change is intended to access a regime hidden by large-black-hole dominance in the canonical ensemble.

Integrate charged fermionic instanton zero modes to obtain six-quark or trilinear superpotentials and neutrino mass operators; track axionic transformations to discuss gauge invariance and Stückelberg masses.
Use a massive-vector Yukawa potential for macroscopic B−L sources and a two-polarization oscillation probability including Majorana mixing, background potential and neutron Zeeman energy.
In four dimensions, extend the N=4 theory from six to 6+N vector multiplets, adding 3N position and 3N Yang–Mills scalars, and compute spectra using the embedding-tensor scalar potential.
Expand the D6 DBI and Wess–Zumino actions to quadratic order about Y=y+2=0. Linear terms cancel, and the quadratic potential and kinetic coefficient determine the normalized position-mode mass.
Extend seven-dimensional half-maximal gauged supergravity from three to 3+N vector multiplets, supplying 3N D6 position scalars; evaluate the scalar Hessian with its noncanonical kinetic metric.
Fix constant lapse, integrate the quadratic background variable q exactly, select the perturbation solution by finite classical action, and evaluate the remaining lapse integral semiclassically.

Picard–Lefschetz theory decomposes a contour into contributing steepest-descent thimbles using intersections with upward flows. Cauchy deformation requires analyticity and negligible endpoint arcs; small complex deformations resolve coincident thimbles.

Numerical shooting treats the full Bianchi IX equations for two symmetry-preserving l=2 modes. Higher harmonics retain linear perturbation equations and second-order backreaction on q; changing to χ=qφ extends the numerical treatment near the real lapse axis.

Canonical oscillator quantization and Virasoro physical-state constraints determine the spectrum. A covariant treatment including asymmetric b,c ghost vacua determines intercepts; comparison with the light-cone result fixes the critical dimension.

Master vertex operators generate tree correlators; Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff manipulations handle zero modes, moduli integrals produce gamma functions, and three-point amplitudes test pole factorization. The torus calculation uses an operator trace with state-norm normalization.

Enumerate Lorentz-invariant on-shell cubic amplitudes using auxiliary null, transverse polarization vectors and homogeneity constraints. Identical massive spin-2 particles admit five structures Ai with derivative counts 0, 2, 2, 4, 6 and dimensionless coefficients ai.

Fourier-transform the eikonal t-channel tree amplitude into impact-parameter space. Complex transverse-momentum deformation isolates on-shell cubic residues; momentum factors become derivatives acting on a massive Bessel-function propagator. Diagonalize the polarization matrix order by order at small mb.

Appendix A derives matrix exponentiation of ladder and crossed-ladder graphs within specified eikonal rules. A separate dRGT calculation diagonalizes fluctuation equations across a shockwave to compare the resulting phase shifts.

Estimate lightest KK/winding masses from shortest lattice vectors, using Minkowski's theorem for a general bound and sharper estimates near large imaginary modulus and cusps. Requiring these masses above Λ truncates the throats.

Compute vertical and circular-arc geodesic lengths in hyperbolic geometry. For cutoff-restricted spaces, introduce d*: infimum of ambient-extension distances, effectively collapsing the boundary; and d#: distance undefined unless a connecting geodesic remains inside the restricted space.

Use the GVW superpotential and Kähler potential, then transform the flux matrix A under modular transformations of the first two tori. Flux-preserving transformations determine the enlarged fundamental domain.

The review evaluates scalar energy density, pressure and w algebraically, then relates the sign of ρ+P to kinetic energy and the null energy condition. Changing the kinetic-term sign supplies the simplest algebraic phantom construction.

Its literature assessment uses nonlinear caustics, gradient and quantum-state stability, vacuum decay, radiative corrections, propagation speeds and S-matrix analyticity. Apparent-phantom examples are assessed through altered supernova luminosities, modified Friedmann equations or assumptions in fitting w.

Jordan-frame entropy conservation converts numerical evolution to temperature. The modified expansion rate enters the Boltzmann equation for Y=nχ/s̃ and x=mχ/T̃. Cross sections are adjusted to the paper's target Ω₀=0.27, with illustrated dark-matter masses from 10 to 5000 GeV.

The authors numerically solve coupled equations for H and dimensionless scalar ϕ; the disformal term prevents eliminating H into a single scalar equation. Initial H is selected from a cubic in H², retaining real positive roots whose evolution satisfies the constraints; viable examples use initial γ near one.

Remove the lifting source, verify that the other fields remain stabilized, then restore it as a deformation. This tests whether the inflaton mass can be reduced independently of the heavy-field metric scale and compactification control.

Minimize heavy fields at each inflaton displacement within one specified sector, declaring how remaining axions are treated. Integrate the resulting axion metric to estimate backreaction; comparisons of different flux choices or lifting couplings are separate operations.

Represent the scalar potential through several top-form couplings and eliminate the forms while retaining their field-dependent kinetic matrix. In the reviewed application, dimensional reduction supplies the matrix and flux-dependent invariant polynomials.

Gravitational waves are computed from scalar anisotropic stress at leading order in gravitational coupling, evolving an auxiliary tensor and extracting its transverse-traceless part in Fourier space at output.

Modified LatticeEasy simulations evolve the nonlinear scalar equations and averaged Friedmann equation. Initial vacuum fluctuations have Rayleigh-distributed magnitudes and uniform random phases. Linear perturbation equations are used where nonlinear effects are not expected.

Numerical Floquet analysis of linear fluctuations around periodic Minkowski-space backgrounds identifies instability bands. Growth rates large compared with H are treated as indicators of amplification in an expanding universe, rather than direct expanding-background solutions.

Find extrema by constrained optimization with P−N Lagrange multipliers. A quadratic expansion gives analytic approximate minimum locations and energies through a coupling-dependent nonorthogonal projector. Convex-polytope lattice sampling supplies statistical samples without enumerating every tile.

Embed the cosine arguments in P auxiliary coordinates φ, restricting a separable cosine potential to Σ=colsp(Q), or its phase-translated counterpart. Intersections with auxiliary cubes define tiles. Extend the exact-period lattice basis to a unimodular integer basis and reduce transverse projections using lattice reduction, including extended LLL.

Toric intersection data, Stanley–Reisner ideals and cohomCalg divisor analysis identify suitable geometries. Orientifold fixed loci, tadpoles, flux-induced charges and intersection indices determine the brane construction, FI constraint and chiral spectrum.

LVS stabilisation and single-field slow-roll estimates are supplemented by numerical evolution of (τ7,V,τ1) with the curved scalar metric and its Christoffel symbols. Evolution uses N=ln a; illustrated trajectories start with zero velocities and orthogonal fields at their fibre-dependent minima.

Derivative linear functionals and semidefinite programming seek positivity on the vacuum and all states outside a proposed target region. A functional normalized to ρ(vac)=1 produces a contradiction if no target state exists. Continuous-charge positivity is implemented through a restricted sum-of-squares search using SDPB.

Extremal-functional zeros supply candidate dimensions and charges. Fixing a discrete spectral pattern and allowed spins turns reconstruction of occupation numbers into linear programming; finite-dimensional projections and spectral Ansätze qualify uniqueness statements.

The transformation-law argument uses a background-gauge-field effective action, maps current correlators to a cylinder and extracts the background-dependent ground-state energy. For constant nonabelian sources, contractions with antisymmetric structure constants eliminate higher connected contributions.

Motivations use long-range force balance, stable charged bound states, species counting and extremal-black-hole decay. Quantum control is explored with schematic one-loop estimates and a supersymmetric completion of the five-dimensional example.

Classical circle reduction evaluates the charge norm and mass derivatives entering Q² ≥ m² + g^{ij}∂i m∂j m, including both axion and dilaton forces. Scalar and fermion reductions are reported to give the same bound.

The Higgsing argument restricts gauge fields to the kernel of the Higgs-charge matrix, projects the charge lattice and current/coupling matrices, and then changes basis so the surviving charge lattice again has integer normalization.

Worldsheet current normalization, modular-invariance results for a superextremal sublattice, the string mass formula and gauge conformal weights provide the spectrum constraints. Kac–Moody central-charge accounting bounds the number of available U(1) factors.

Analyses use weighted means, joint likelihoods and marginalization; spatial fits compare A cos Ψ with A ln(1+z) cos Ψ. Atomic clocks constrain frequency-ratio drifts through coupling sensitivities, while future sensitivities are assessed with Fisher matrices.

Spectroscopy separates redshift from coupling-induced shifts using transitions with different sensitivity coefficients, provided they originate at the same location. It requires accurate laboratory wavelengths, sensitivity calculations and attention to isotopic abundances.

Use Fourier-space linear perturbations in Newtonian gauge, including vierbein gauge fixing. Recast the stress tensor as a real fluid with anisotropic stress, then combine analytic constraints with numerical evolution for longitudinal and orthogonal wavevectors.

Vary the first-order action, solve algebraically for contortion, and rewrite the Einstein–Dirac equations using torsion-free quantities. Fierz identities and Clifford-algebra projections express spinor dynamics entirely through bilinears.

Corrections to K are used with the supersymmetric scalar-potential formula and perturbative nonrenormalization of W to diagnose a physical potential. An explicit sextic-fourfold example uses adjunction and obtains ∫M J∧c3=−420, illustrating a nonzero perturbative correction.

Power counting combines flux quantization, the M2-charge tadpole and the higher-derivative expansion. The analysis compares flux stress-energy, R⁴ interactions and their supersymmetric flux completions, including contributions at matching orders from different derivative orders.

Gaussian integration exchanges numerator and denominator determinants relative to ordinary-statistics U(N), giving inverse partition functions. The mass-dependent product is evaluated numerically through the second derivative of the free energy.

Reverse chiral-superfield statistics: physical scalars and auxiliary scalars anticommute, while spinors commute. Couple these multiplets to background vector multiplets and supergravity to organize supersymmetric spin 0–2 deformations.

Enumerate SO(10) tops and their dual polytopes; extract coefficient factorizations and Weierstrass vanishing orders. Resolve fibers, identify split rational curves, and intersect them with Shioda divisors to obtain Abelian charges; Weierstrass orders alone do not distinguish these charges.

Use toric Chern classes, adjunction and quotient intersection rings modulo linear equivalences and Stanley–Reissner ideals to obtain Euler numbers and neutral matter. The authors implement Gröbner reduction in SAGE; multisection models require an ambient-space computation rather than the section adjunction identity.

Compute multiplicities through base intersections and resultants, subtracting embedded singlet and SO(10) matter loci with their multiplicities. When direct resultants are computationally infeasible, unhiggs to simpler singlet ideals and infer spectra through Higgs transitions.

Select α=0, β=1 by agreement of the three coupling extractions for the chosen regulator and perturbative approximation. Integrate hypercharge flow using imported single-metric gravitational beta functions with minimally coupled matter and ηh=0.

Extract the gauge beta function independently from scalar–photon three-point and four-point vertices and the photon propagator. Including field anomalous dimensions recovers the known gravity-free one-loop result βρ=ρ³/(48π²); also examine a transverse-traceless-only gravity approximation.

Project the Wetterich functional RG equation onto a finite effective-action truncation. Use a linear background split g=ḡ+h, flat auxiliary background, wave-function renormalizations and a theta regulator Rk=Z(k²−p²)θ(k²−p²).

Infer gauge algebras and candidate matter from discriminant vanishing orders, codimension-two enhancements and adjoint branching; determine multiplicities with six-dimensional gauge anomalies and geometric genera. Euler-characteristic stratification supplies the gravitational-anomaly analysis.

Use the fiberwise elliptic-curve group law to identify torsion points, impose their coordinates on the Morrison–Park section, and solve the resulting polynomial identities by coprime factorization in local unique factorization domains. Global validity requires compatible line bundles and sections.

For the restricted model, use toric blow-ups, Stanley–Reisner relations, prime ideals and integral divisor–curve intersections to determine the quotient group. Smith normal form tracks Higgsing of abelian factors and possible residual discrete symmetries.

Continue fully nonlinear hairy solutions and, at fixed amplitude above amax, lower q while monitoring K=L⁴RabcdRabcd outside the horizon. Estimate the singular threshold qc by linear extrapolation of the inverse maximum curvature.

Find static normalizable scalar zero modes through the generalized eigenvalue problem (∇²-m²)Φ=q²AaAaΦ. Check instability onset with the lowest quasinormal frequency: for perturbations e^(-iωt), positive Im ω denotes growth.

Solve the static Einstein–DeTurck elliptic equations by a Newton-like method, using pure AdS as reference metric. With matter, exclusion of non-Einstein DeTurck solutions is not supplied by the cited theorem; the prescribed check is χ=ξaξa→0 in the continuum limit.

Reduce the spatial integrations to overlap volumes of two balls, then evaluate temporal integrations by contour methods with the positive-energy iε prescription. Optimize the expansion rate of the measurement sphere to suppress fluctuations.

Compute vacuum charge and energy fluctuations by integrating current-current and stress-tensor two-point functions over time-smeared balls. Gauss's law identifies electric flux with a volume charge operator; an approximate gravitational Gauss law supplies the mass volume operator.

Extract gravitational running using a four-sphere background with vanishing background scalar and heat-kernel techniques. Extract scalar wave-function and higher-derivative running from q² and q⁴ terms in flat-background scalar two-point diagrams.

Use a Litim regulator and a distributional external-momentum expansion that retains integration-boundary contributions. The appendix adopts Θ(0) = 1/2; surface terms affect higher-order kinetic terms but not the scalar anomalous dimension.

Project the functional renormalization group equation for the effective average action onto the retained gravitational and scalar operators. The regulator vanishes as k → 0, where Γk becomes the ordinary effective action.

Transform the crossed harmonic, pair it with each target harmonic and divide by the target norm. The paper applies this operation to identity and O2 exchange, using the supplied degree-four polynomials for explicit channels.

Subtract KK bubble and tadpole self-energies evaluated with the two phi2 quantizations, then extract the induced single-trace shift. A CFT alternative convolves a UV mixed four-point function with the auxiliary propagator.

Intersect protected UV multiplets with unmixed sectors and subtract the known zero UV term. The visually confirmed even-p A-series parity conflict makes unrestricted application conditional on clarifying the primary identification.
Compare probe-M2 self-energies or forces using the two phi2 quantizations. Residual flat directions may require higher-loop interactions with the entire KK tower.
Apply the singlet double-trace deformation to every stress-primary component. Holographically this replaces dimension-one by dimension-two boundary conditions for the m²L²=−2 scalar multiplet.

Extract leading-twist logarithms, invert their collinear-block expansion and normalize by mean-field OPE weights. Individual binding corrections require nondegeneracy; complete dimensions additionally require the constituent single-trace shifts.
Change every scalar quantization below Δ=3/2, then inspect remaining BF-saturating modes and symmetry-preserving deformations. This is a preliminary extension of the ABJM operation.
Introduce the auxiliary field for O and take the IR Legendre transform of the UV connected functional. This constructs leading IR correlators without a separate microscopic IR Lagrangian.
Attach sigma kernels to the flowing external legs of the UV correlator and integrate over their attachment points. Star-triangle identities determine the IR coefficient and its singular limits.

Reviews the Margolus-Levitin overlap argument and extends it to approximate orthogonality. Lloyd's operation-counting bound is obtained by applying the orthogonalization-time bound to each elementary gate, including commuting parallel gates.

Estimates thermal-field-double overlaps using a continuum spectral density exp S(E) and a quadratic entropy saddle. This gives Gaussian overlap decay and τcoh = sqrt(-S''(E)); comparison with τcomp = (dC/dt)^(-1) diagnoses a serial gate's action. Charge fluctuations require an entropy-Hessian or Gibbs-free-energy treatment.

Uses black-hole thought experiments, quantum duality examples, and a qualitative AdS/CFT argument: couple a boundary global symmetry to a background gauge field, then integrate over its possible bulk extensions to obtain a dynamical bulk gauge field.

Classifies possible symmetry violations by gauge invariance and operator dimension. Renormalization-group reasoning distinguishes renormalizable interactions from irrelevant operators suppressed by heavy scales and motivates interpreting apparent conservation laws as low-energy accidents.

Defines an IR contour quantity ΣIR from the forward amplitude divided by (s−μ²)^3, including light poles and the subtraction point. Cauchy deformation, crossing, real analyticity, the asymptotic bound, and the optical theorem express it as a positive dispersive integral.

Retains calculable elastic or inelastic IR cross-sections below an energy E and discards positive higher-energy contributions. For massive gravity, computes polarization amplitudes and optimizes the smallest of five functions Fi over the positivity-allowed potential parameters to obtain a conservative mass/coupling bound.
TT-mode projections distinguish the nonminimal four-derivative vertex □hTTμν φ∂μ∂νφ from the independent hTTμν φ∂μ∂ν□φ structure. The latter, associated with a scalar φΔ²φ operator, is projected out.
Project the Wetterich equation using a simultaneous vertex and derivative expansion. The computed running quantities are ηTT, ηTr, ηφ and the one-graviton/two-scalar couplings g3 and σ3.

Use a spectrally adjusted Litim-type regulator with shape r(z) = (1 − z)θ(1 − z)/z. Compare LO with all anomalous dimensions zero, NLO with anomalous dimensions omitted from regulator scale derivatives, and the full anomalous-dimension dependence.

Vary the metric and connection independently in constrained metric-affine actions. The torsion-based discussion uses the Bianchi identity to eliminate multiplier dependence; in the symmetric teleparallel case the multipliers do not enter the metric equations.

Parameterize the flat torsionless connection with fields ξλ, choose its vanishing-connection gauge, and expand gμν = ημν + hμν to quadratic order. Compare the resulting kinetic structure with the conditions for linearized diffeomorphism invariance.

Evaluate f(Q) theories on spatially flat FLRW backgrounds to obtain modified Friedmann equations. The continuity equation is obtained from the corresponding Bianchi identities as a consistency check of the background ansatz.

The imported Elitzur–Nair method embeds G in a larger group F, relates a global G anomaly to a local F anomaly through Chern–Simons descent, and fixes normalization using representation branching and the homotopy long exact sequence for G→F→F/G.

Spectral flow, the mod-2 Dirac index and the APS η invariant describe anomaly phases. For the proposed Sp(N) cancellation, KO-theoretic Poincaré duality retains the spin structure of the instanton locus, and KO integration encodes the relevant indices.

The instanton method decomposes RG under SU(2)×H and introduces a unit-charge codimension-four instanton. An n-dimensional SU(2) representation supplies Nn=(n³−n)/6 zero modes; their H representations define a lower-dimensional fermion theory whose anomaly diagnoses an anomaly of the original theory.

Use the T-BMT spin equation with a time-dependent EDM parameter, under β·E=β·B=0. Tune E, B and beam momentum so the horizontal spin-precession frequency relative to momentum matches the target axion frequency while retaining the chosen bending radius.

Infer vertical precession from carbon-polarimeter left/right scattering asymmetry, ε(t)=PAθ(t). Simulated asymmetry is fitted using linear growth and polarization decay; the frequency uncertainty is converted through σd=(sℏ/E*)σωd.

Integrate the spin and velocity equations to study phase dependence. Separate frequency-search procedures use repeated frozen-spin measurements and sinusoidal fits at low frequency, or discrete resonant settings separated by half an axion linewidth at high frequency.
