Enumerate origins at fixed stack number and hypercharge, calculate projected consistency charges, and identify extra fields that can cancel residual contributions.
Choose a visible sector, identify possible mediator paths, and use masses and couplings to assess communication.
Specify an allowed instanton sector, construct the Higgs-dependent cosine operator, and evaluate its curvature after symmetry breaking. Keep the actual coefficient when interpreting the mass.

Inspect a trained classifier to formulate a conjecture, then establish it independently before exhaustive counting. The useful transition is from an empirical decision pattern to a proved combinatorial condition.

Expand internal components of C_p in a cohomology basis and retain spacetime-dependent coefficients. Account for projections, gauging, and lifting before identifying the resulting physical axion spectrum.
Compute orders, consult the Kodaira dictionary, and resolve remaining algebra ambiguities using additional geometric data.

Attach classified height-at-most-six trees to all triangulation edges and faces, then perform their blowups. The construction produces candidate bases satisfying the specified divisorial singularity criterion.
Compute triangle areas and multiply their exponential factors, after testing the perturbative selection rules.

Use Hamiltonian constraints to integrate out radial gravitational degrees of freedom, obtaining a nonlocal spherical-shell action. WKB mode functions and saddle-point Bogoliubov integrals implement initial plane-wave conditions selecting the freely falling Unruh vacuum.

Evaluate the imaginary canonical action using Hamilton's equations and outgoing null trajectories in Painlevé–Gullstrand coordinates. The future-positive-energy contour prescription is ω→ω−iε; logarithmic branch cuts provide an alternative evaluation.

Regulate extremality before taking the limit, use Israel thin-wall junction conditions to define near-horizon shell energy, and compare Euclidean throat geometries and multicenter solutions with gravitational instantons.

Exploit fibration or covering structure to find effective curves missed by toric-surface intersections. Degenerate fibre components, lifted base curves and special covering fibres produce extra inequalities that can remove apparently infinite directions.

Construct both cone approximations, dualize them, impose stabilization constraints, and integrate the induced metric. Refine the outer Kähler domain when its length diverges, because a divergent overestimate cannot decide whether the physical domain has finite range.

Compute divisor topology, identify rigid del Pezzos, and impose a rank-one volume-polynomial test before classifying fibrations. The operation uses topological features to select candidate stabilization geometries instead of requiring a preselected simplified intersection polynomial.

Compute the full Hessian, impose tangent constraints, and integrate its pullback over the cone-allowed interval. The paper uses this standard operation to obtain explicit distances for SSC, K3 and SSC-like geometries, while treating structureless cases implicitly.

Intersect the cone-allowed trajectory with global compactification, amplitude, stability, reheating and scale-separation requirements. The procedure treats these as simultaneous conditions, including the post-inflationary minimum rather than only the slow-roll plateau.

Replace explicit polynomial elimination by geometric boundary checks. A finite parameter interval and a bounded induced metric imply finite proper length, provided all components and endpoint behavior have been accounted for.

The method of characteristics identifies an effective metric for scalar fluctuations. Numerical background integration follows the coefficient Δ(t) multiplying φ̈, the effective sound speed, and transitions between singular and oscillatory solutions.

Slow-roll background relations and imported perturbation-spectrum formulas are used to calculate the scalar tilt, running, tensor spectrum, and tensor-to-scalar ratio. A field-excursion expansion in e-folds gives a modified Lyth-bound analysis.

Oscillatory reheating is constrained through cosmological scale matching and entropy conservation. Nonoscillatory branches are assessed with estimates of nonadiabatic particle production, decay, and energy transfer at the inflaton's first zero crossing.

A fixed-charge canonical Euclidean path integral compares the heavy-field classical solution with an off-shell configuration having all heavy fields frozen to zero. A local-minimum assumption supplies an action inequality and hence a lower free energy.
Thermodynamic identities retain the inverse-temperature shift Δβ=∂_MΔS when translating a same-temperature free-energy comparison into an entropy comparison at fixed mass and charge.

The authors perturb the Reissner-Nordström metric to first order in operator coefficients and evaluate Wald entropy. They separate explicit interaction corrections from the horizon-area shift, then use the perturbed horizon condition to relate entropy and extremality.

The present GW energy density is estimated using an imported analytic gauge-mode formula evaluated with numerical H(N) and ξ(N), rather than by solving the tensor equation jointly with the gauge modes. Frequencies are mapped from horizon-exit scales.

An approximate particular solution for gauge-sourced inflaton fluctuations gives an induced curvature spectrum, added to the vacuum contribution. PBH abundances use the imported non-Gaussian prescription ζ=g²−⟨g²⟩ for Gaussian g and a threshold-tail integral.

The inflaton is split into a homogeneous mean and fluctuations. Circularly polarized gauge-mode equations are evolved with gauge-field expectation values feeding back into the mean-field and Friedmann equations, retaining a linear treatment of the modes.

Compare tree-level and explicit one-/two-loop toy-model vacuum-energy distributions; use semianalytic compactification solutions, vacuum-energy quantiles and modulus-mass estimates to characterize the string-model examples.

Solve the flux-dependent potential for classically stable local minima, map each solution to Λ, and construct a weighted delta-function distribution over flux choices. Some choices have no minimum and others have multiple minima.

The authors use stationary-point conditions and the scalar Hessian to extract masses. Separately, they diagonalize the zeroth partial-wave matrix for nonlinear-sigma Goldstone scattering and impose |Re a0| ≤ 1/2.

Renormalized perturbation theory includes the required quartic counterterm. The effective potential combines the μ bilinear, λ|Φ1†Φ2|² and a field-dependent contribution Δ(ĥ)ĥ⁴. Gauge and top loops are evaluated in Landau gauge and the MS scheme.

Vary the energy functional by inserting real sources for arbitrary operators; metric variations are included through stress-tensor insertions. Reflection symmetry combines bra and ket variations into twice an integrated connected stress-tensor–operator correlator.

For a free conformally coupled scalar, compare the canonical Gaussian vacuum wave-functional with the Gaussian obtained from a filling. The latter requires restricting the propagator to the boundary before taking its inverse; spectral compatibility conditions are then stated.

Compare the energy of the hemisphere-times-circle state with the torus Casimir energy. Stress-tensor symmetry and tracelessness relate its energy to the thermal energy on a sphere: Eψ = −(πL1/2L2)Eth, with sphere radius L2 and inverse temperature 2πL1.

The authors apply Osterwalder–Schrader reflection positivity and the requirement of a Källén–Lehmann representation with nonnegative spectral density. A negative reflected quadratic form would produce a negative norm in the standard Euclidean reconstruction.

For the scalar diagonal test they use a nonnegative Gaussian-mixture representation when 0 < s ≤ 1, invoking Bernstein’s theorem. For s > 1 they present numerical behavior and invoke cited analytic arguments; the all-s spectral obstruction is attributed to an imported Widder theorem.

Erasure correction is analyzed through logical-operator reconstruction, reference-system decoupling and encoding unitaries. Entropy inequalities yield m ≥ (n+k)/2 for n physical qudits, k logical qudits and threshold m, under the stated symmetry of recoverability.

The three-qutrit code and HaPPY tensor network illustrate redundant encoding. HaPPY uses six-index perfect tensors on a hyperbolic pentagon tiling, with operator pushing implementing reconstruction; random tensors provide an approximate complementary-recovery construction at large bond dimension.

Perturbative reconstruction combines normal-mode inversion and the extrapolate dictionary with an iterative spacelike Green-function solution of bulk operator equations. Interaction coefficients must match CFT correlators to obtain the required spacelike commutators.
Weinberg’s adiabatic-mode construction supplements the temporal transformation with a residual spatial diffeomorphism so that the lapse and shift constraint solutions remain preserved.

Stückelberg restoration introduces the time-translation Goldstone π. Background tadpole equations and symmetry recursions determine leading-derivative interactions; canonical normalization and dimensional analysis estimate non-Gaussianity and strong coupling.

The authors impose the combined internal shift and temporal diffeomorphism preserving unitary gauge. In clock coordinates, symmetry makes coefficients of full geometric operators time independent; re-expansion around the background yields recursion relations for perturbative coefficients.

Construct boundary-anchored line dressings by locating the scalar along a perpendicular geodesic, solving the transformation to Fefferman–Graham gauge hρμ=0, and undoing that transformation. Angular averaging gives the temporal Coulomb dressing; its spatial part is fixed by the required gauge transformation.

Evaluate dressing fields through metric–dressed-operator commutators using ADM canonical quantization. Derive AdS charges through the covariant canonical formalism, Noether charge, symplectic potential, and gravitational constraints.

Integrate out massive matter using the one-loop heat-kernel expansion. Leading equations of motion and field redefinitions convert curvature corrections into F⁴ operators in 3D; a Weyl-tensor–F² operator also remains in 4D.
Test subluminality through kinetic-matrix eigenvalues: dualize photons to scalars in 3D; in 4D use a thermal photon gas and geometric optics to avoid photon–graviton kinetic mixing.

Use crossing-symmetric forward amplitudes, a contour integral of M(s)/s³, Schwarz reflection, a Froissart-bound assumption, and the optical theorem to relate four-derivative coefficients to nonnegative spectral integrals.

Combine modular S/T transformations with crossing and lasso operations to constrain defect spins, integral defect-state multiplicities, and bulk traces. Bootstrap IR Frobenius algebras using these constraints and associativity; bulk OPE associativity alone does not fix all resulting structure constants.

Use locality, cutting and sewing, and partial fusion to derive H-junction crossing and the pentagon identity. Crossing kernels are studied modulo changes of junction basis; selected low-rank solutions are obtained after gauge fixing, including implementation in Mathematica.

Appendix B supplies first-order systems stated to be numerically integrated for d=7 solutions with SU(2) vectors. The packet provides equations and one plot caption, without enough information to reproduce the integrations.

Set the linearized fermionic supersymmetry variations to zero for nonzero Killing spinors, obtaining first-order BPS equations. Spinor bilinears generate Killing vectors and support classifications with specified isometries.

Use Kaluza–Klein mode expansions and reduction ansätze; twisted reductions retain left-invariant forms on an internal group manifold. The review presents left invariance as the reason these twisted reductions are consistent truncations.

Current Ward identities are analyzed through momentum-space Lorentz decompositions and Bose symmetry. Characteristic three-point functions are simplified at p²=q²=(p+q)²=Q²; polynomial contact terms are distinguished from nonanalytic contributions.
Background-field couplings, six-form anomaly polynomials, descent, five-dimensional anomaly inflow and local counterterms organize the anomaly analysis.

Resolve by ambient blowups centered successively at (x,y,s) and (x,y,t), or in reverse order. Use the Jacobian criterion for smoothness and a common conifold-type partial resolution to exhibit the Atiyah flop.
Apply imported blowup Chern-class and Chow-pushforward formulas to Euler characteristics and cubic intersections; use Shioda–Tate–Wazir and Noether’s formula for Hodge numbers.

Compute curve weights as negative intersections with non-affine fibral divisors; saturate the weight set to identify representations. Weight kernels define the arrangement I(g,R) inside the dual fundamental Weyl chamber.

The described Higgs-mass calculation starts with the high-scale soft-breaking Lagrangian and quartic coupling, matches to an effective theory near the geometric mean of stop masses, integrates out heavier scalars, and runs to the top scale. Two-loop threshold corrections and three-loop beta functions are mentioned as available inputs.

The argument combines four qualitative clues: a supersymmetric Higgs-mass upper bound, a supersymmetric hierarchy solution, Standard-Model-like branching ratios in the decoupling limit, and cosmological vacuum stability. No quantitative model-selection statistic is supplied.

Dimensional reduction of democratic massive IIA supergravity with Lagrange multipliers enforcing Bianchi identities and Hodge duality; reduction of D6 Chern–Simons couplings and elimination of nonpropagating four-forms.

The authors also calculate the N=1 supergravity F-term potential using the proposed holomorphic fields, inverse Kähler metrics and homogeneity identities, reporting agreement with dimensional reduction under simplifying metric assumptions.

Poincare duality, relative homology, and Hodge decomposition organize charges, boundary-preserving gauge transformations, and the gauge condition d†A=f. Higher p requires a tower of gauge-of-gauge fixing and ghosts.
Gaussian Wilson-brane expectation values and Abelian duality diagnose infrared fluctuations. For compact theories, a generalized Polyakov instanton argument supplies a separate confinement mechanism.
A spectral commutator argument combines a nonzero charged expectation value, current conservation, and a charge-support boundary disjoint from the operator to motivate gaplessness.

Construct monodromy orbits of massless charges and quotient M by the type II sublattice MII. Analyze central-charge phases and walls of marginal stability to motivate interpreting distinct quotient classes as stable BPS candidates.
Compute one-loop threshold corrections to scalar and gauge kinetic terms, summing tower states below a field-dependent cutoff. The species scale supplies the proposed ultraviolet matching scale.

Schmid’s nilpotent orbit theorem supplies local periods Π=exp(tN)A with holomorphic A and polynomial leading e^(−K). The SL2-orbit theorem, monodromy weight filtration and Deligne splitting control positivity, charge decomposition and Hodge-norm growth.

Expand about a fixed background, normalize the scalar kinetic term, estimate each state’s propagator correction, and sum states below the probing energy. Solve λ_φ≈1 to estimate strong coupling. The operation retains spectral thresholds but discards numerical factors and detailed loop functions.

The states are also constructed as ultraviolet-suppressed squeezed Bunch-Davies states. For non-Gaussianity, a previously calculated high-frequency three-point correction is translated into boundary-state parameters and evaluated in the folded limit.

The excited-state stress tensor, obtained from the corrected two-point function, measures backreaction via Ehrenfest's theorem. Bounds enforce perturbativity, slow roll, and approximately scale-invariant observable perturbations.

An imported boundary-action formalism encodes initial conditions in a quadratic spatial kernel κ. Variation yields (∂n+κ)φ=0; κ=κBD+δκ determines Bogoliubov mixing. Moving the boundary requires changing κ to preserve the physical modes.

The imported momentum-transfer cross section has Coulomb scaling σ̄t=2πα²ε²ξ/(μχ,t²v⁴). Debye screening regulates the forward divergence; the logarithm is approximated as nearly constant over the relevant era.

Approximate annihilation rates and a constant freeze-out parameter estimate thermal relic production and dark-radiation constraints. The displayed thermal-relic line assumes fdm=1 and annihilation into electron-positron pairs, with dark-sector interactions omitted.

Coupled evolution equations track baryon and charged-DM temperatures, ionization fraction, and relative velocity, including Hubble cooling, drag, and Compton exchange. Solutions are averaged over a Maxwell-Boltzmann initial streaming distribution with rms 29 km/s at decoupling.

For axions, integrate production weighted by energy-dependent escape probability rather than impose blackbody emission at large coupling. Multiply the leading nuclear rate by low-energy-cutoff, finite-pion-mass/degeneracy and higher-order spin-response factors, using imported N3LO chiral-EFT results.

Propose a trapping diagnostic based on an expected π/2 angular deflection during a random walk from the decoupling radius outward. Locate the large-coupling boundary by matching thermal dark-sector luminosity to Lν and finding the coupling producing that deflection; one scatter is inadequate for forward-peaked elastic scattering.

Calculate dark-sector production from neutron–proton bremsstrahlung through on- or off-shell A′ and thermal SM-photon decay. Interaction-basis amplitudes retain distinct longitudinal and transverse photon polarization tensors and plasma resonances.

The paper reviews the superspace dualization of ordinary chiral supergravity: replace selected superpotential constants by three-form field strengths encoded through complex linear superfields. Its bosonic treatment integrates out four-forms, retaining the boundary term, to recover W=e_I f^I−m^I G_I and the conventional scalar potential.

Membrane couplings are constructed with superspace differential forms and checked by a projected κ-variation. Domain-wall equations follow from vanishing fermion variations and alternatively from completing the reduced action into squares, including localized sources and the Gibbons–Hawking term.

PBH abundance is estimated from a Gaussian tail above a collapse threshold, using its rare-event approximation. Horizon-mass matching and radiation-era redshifting relate formation abundance to dark matter today. The text also distinguishes a narrow mass estimate from an integrated, broadly peaked mass function.

The authors solve the Mukhanov–Sasaki equation for rescaled curvature modes with Bunch–Davies initial conditions. They evaluate the power spectrum at the end of inflation because modes can grow outside the horizon during the transient constant-roll phase, and compare this with the horizon-exit slow-roll estimate.

Construct a suitable nonabelian model, use two adjoints to break to U(1), and read the daughter charge spectrum. The source supplies an existence outline, while leaving the explicit abelian geometry and charge branching unshown.

Enumerate admissible U(1) spectra, apply the exchangeability, SU(2) NGIN, and SU(2) gravitational tests independently, then count each three-bit class. Reproduction requires the omitted test definitions and anomaly equations.

Solve abelian moment constraints 6γ = Σ(q>0)xq q² and 3ñ = Σ(q>0)xq q⁴, together with H − V + 29T = 273 and nonnegative integer multiplicities. For one U(1), V = 1 and H counts neutral plus charged hypermultiplets.

Search broader toric and complete-intersection fiber classes, or extend non-UFD constructions directly and through Higgsing exotic nonabelian matter. The source presents these as research strategies, with charge-three toric examples as precedent.
Use explicit integer charge families and finite charge-cutoff enumerations, supplemented by continuum estimates of lattice points on the intersection of a sphere and quartic hypersurface.

Organize spectra through anomaly-equivalent exchanges, such as 10 neutral hypers + 6 charge-2 hypers ↔ 1 charge-3 hyper + 15 charge-1 hypers. Nonnegativity must be checked; these formal exchanges need not correspond to physical transitions.

Start from an SU(N) model with suitable adjoints, Higgs to the specified U(1), and translate its anomaly coefficient with the stated generator normalization. The operation applies only when that Higgsing route exists.
Solve coupled scalar and Einstein equations order by order in radial powers and logarithms around KS, using a flat domain-wall ansatz; compare with supersymmetric gradient-flow equations.

Derive Ward identities from invariance of the renormalized action under gauge-preserving bulk supersymmetry and radial diffeomorphisms. Obtain bosonic vevs by functional differentiation, using the flat-domain-wall counterterm Sct=−∫√−γ 2W.

Linearize around asymptotic KS to identify sources, then diagonalize their mixing through hatted combinations. Use leading falloffs directly when covariant composite-field definitions are inconvenient or nonunique.

Construct the charge-dependent integrand, evaluate it in the desired phase, and differentiate -log Z. The resulting metric initially uses FI coordinates; identifying volume coordinates requires additional coordinate matching and mirror-period information.
Partition the total occupation, count monomial choices, and retain factorial weights. Correct index handling and sector admissibility must be checked before the result is used in reduced periods.

Construct the metric from periods, integrate specified paths, and solve geodesics on invariant asymptotic slices. Treat convergence, approximation control, and global minimality as separate requirements.
The imported LG series is continued and reorganized to make other regimes accessible. For k_1=1 the initial type is (d+1)F_d; parameter cancellation reduces the examples to at most type (13,12).
Identify coefficients within each orbit, retain representative periods with multiplicities, and aggregate occupation sums. The packet does not demonstrate a complete sector-aware implementation.

The reported search minimizes squared residuals plus a linear coefficient term. Its interpretation requires normalization, residual verification, and endpoint selection information absent from the packet.
Sum weighted admissible occupation allocations into periods, then form the signed gamma-weighted quadratic expression for the Kähler potential.

Differentiate the analytically continued coefficients, continue both periods, and divide. Direct differentiation requires d Psi(dn+1)-sum_j k_j Psi(k_jn+1), so the source's displayed unweighted coefficient cannot be used interchangeably.

Continue a fundamental period, generate independent solutions, normalize their symplectic lattice, and differentiate the negative logarithm of the consistently conjugated pairing. This also supplies the mirror map, which is harder to extract from the sphere partition function.

Integrate the full geodesic equation, determine which branches remain minimizing, and evaluate the candidate tower along them. Numerical accuracy, chart consistency and validity of the mass approximation are distinct requirements.
Translate B-field gauge shifts into row-vector equations involving period monodromies. Solve them, choose additive constants, and find a compatible symplectic basis for the Kähler pairing.

Compute both singular sets, include subgroup branches, and match distinguished points and normalization. Conflicting polynomial and discriminant data prevent treating this supplied example's final dictionary as verified.

Integrate sampled outgoing trajectories, restore their short omitted origin segments, apply the mirror map, and fit the large-volume primitive. Interpret angular variation and sample averages within the limitations of finite intervals.
Use the three-term U decomposition for large phi or regroup psi powers into 7F6 functions for large psi. Preserve all discriminant inequalities and analytic-continuation branches.

Restricted infinite tensor products of entangled qubit pairs illustrate Type II and Type III factors. The reference vector determines the Hilbert-space completion and therefore which operator sequences converge; changing that reference can change the resulting algebra.

Closed antilinear Tomita operators, polar decomposition, and relative modular operators replace reduced density matrices. Monotonicity is explained through inclusion of closed operator graphs, inequalities for resolvents, and the resulting ordering of logarithms.

Positive energy supplies complex-time holomorphy. Timelike translations and Cauchy continuation extend vanishing matrix elements, yielding the Reeh–Schlieder density argument. For wedges, analytic continuation of Lorentz boosts provides an alternative to the Euclidean path-integral construction.

Resonant conversion is evaluated where the plasma photon mass equals m_A′. The calculation weights conversion by free-free survival P_s≈exp(−τ_ff), then compares added photon counts with the standard CMB count in a specified 21 cm energy window and applies stellar and spectral-distortion constraints.

The authors derive the expanding-universe spectrum from monochromatic decay injection, evaluating H at the production redshift determined by α=m_a(1+z)/(2ω). Conversion multiplies this spectrum by the oscillation probability; subsequent evolution uses x and number-density dilution proportional to (1+z)³.

An effective dimension-five interaction aF′F̃′/(4f_a), together with kinetic mixing −εFF′/2 and a dark-photon mass term, defines the explicit model. The quoted two-body decay rate is Γ_a=m_a³/(64πf_a²).

Reviews the canonical superhorizon amplification mechanism: z=aφ̇/H and z′/z=aH(1+ε−δ). When δ>1+ε, friction changes sign and the normally decaying curvature mode can grow. This is a diagnostic, rather than a quantitative prediction of the enhancement.

Numerically evolves homogeneous equations using N=ln a and computes linearized perturbations with MultiModeCode. Numerical mode evolution replaces horizon-crossing slow-roll estimates where δ varies appreciably.

Estimates PBH abundance using a Press–Schechter Gaussian tail, a power-spectrum-derived smoothed density variance, radiation-era mass–wavenumber matching, and redshifting followed by integration over logarithmic PBH mass.

Adopt rhp=2(M+E) as a hoop radius, split merging into stages before and after crossing it, and compare energies and entropy. Numerical scans supply charge-to-mass thresholds; a linear-in-rotation solution extends the calculation.

Wald-type capture/overcharging thought experiment: compare a particle's horizon-reaching energy with the energy compatible with exposing a singularity, use a small-q expansion, and examine the effective potential for arrival from infinity.

Use the Shioda homomorphism and finite Mordell–Weil component groups to replace a section by a multiple meeting every generic affine fibre component. Combine an effective height-pairing decomposition with contractible-curve classification, rational-singularity cohomology and Riemann–Roch.

Decompose anomaly-coefficient vectors using the moduli-dependent duality matrix D(j)=2j⊗j_flat−1. Compute local anomalies from retained multiplets and project Green–Schwarz coefficients onto the tensor subspace that remains dynamical; this can remove tensors beyond the gravity tensor.

Integrates out H′ at tree level in the most general renormalizable exchange-symmetric two-doublet potential. Studies how extra scalar couplings spoil the link between tuning the light Higgs mass and suppressing its quartic.

Generates dimension-five flavor operators by integrating out heavy vectorlike fermions. Spurion symmetries and loop estimates identify the first non-Hermitian corrections relevant to strong CP, including mixed up/down flavor structures.

Uses one-loop gauge running and matching at v′, quantifying unification through differences or dispersion of 8π²/g_i². Nearly degenerate complete SO(10) multiplets are assumed not to change relative one-loop running.

Orbifold boundary conditions determine which particles possess KK towers. The authors count their bosonic and fermionic contributions and examine small-radius mass expansions, including mass-squared supertraces and logarithmic mass dependence.

Background-field computation of one-loop Casimir potentials, with dimensional or generalized zeta-function regularization. Circle contributions involve modified Bessel K2 functions; torus expressions also involve polylogarithms.

Pure-gravity arguments use on-shell three-point vertices and imported tree-amplitude equivalence. Scalar examples use Fourier integrals evaluated analytically for simple exponential form factors and numerically for the Kuz’min and Tomboulis choices.

The constructive recipe adds terms quadratic in the local seed theory's equations of motion, EFE, and applies a perturbative field redefinition. An explicit gravity–Maxwell–scalar action illustrates the construction; optional supersymmetry supplies another cited realization.

The eikonal approximation resums ladder and crossed-ladder exchange in the Regge limit. The impact-parameter phase is δ(b,s)=(1/2s)∫d^(D−2)q/(2π)^(D−2) exp(iq·b)Atree(s,−q²), and the diagnostic time delay is Δt=2∂Eδ.

The logarithmic ansatz is motivated by bulk closed-string exchange between localized graviton vertices and brane/orientifold sources. A discrete transverse-momentum tadpole sum yields different infrared behavior according to transverse codimension.

Six T-dualities map a type-I D9/D5 toroidal description to the D3/D7 variables. Corrections to the Einstein kinetic term are encoded as shifts of the compactification volume and hence of the Kähler potential.

The authors expand the F- and D-term potentials at large volume, minimize cycle ratios and total volume, and express the volume stationary point through a Lambert W function. The single-brane appendix instead analyzes a rational potential outside its singularities.

Uses exact scattering examples to compare with the general threshold arguments: a_t=(A/2)tanh(x/l), its sharp-step limit, and the gravitational step v(x)=Vθ(x). These are author calculations, not independently reproduced here.

Uses the Feynman prescription m→m−iε and studies branch points pinching the frequency contour. Near the electric threshold, a low-momentum transfer expansion has real coefficients satisfying c₊c₋−c₀c₊₋=1 by current conservation.

Differentiates the one-loop log determinant with respect to m², expresses the Feynman Green function through scattering modes and a Wronskian, and relates the effective action to an integral of log α. Here 1/α is the transmission amplitude.

Translate defect networks and F-moves into simplicial background fields: flat G transition functions A and an A-valued 2-cochain B. Twisted group cohomology, descent, and Bockstein homomorphisms encode their compatibility.

Classify anomalies in dimensions one through four using topological inflow actions modulo local counterterms. Closure is imposed on the total inflow cochain in one further dimension, rather than on each summand separately; 3d anomalies require quadratic refinements and affine Pontryagin squares.

Imported covariant Mukhanov–Sasaki formalism: project perturbations along the velocity and turn directions, include field-space curvature in the mass matrix, and use long-wavelength transfer functions. The authors also report numerical checks of the shifted observable relations with m.transport.

Analytic dominant-balance approximations to the background equations, small-α and large-mass-ratio expansions, and angular integration of H/θ̇ to estimate e-folds. Numerical trajectories and equation-term comparisons support the proposed attractor over sampled initial conditions.

Beyond low energies, the authors solve collective G,Σ Schwinger–Dyson equations numerically and analytically at large q. The latter uses Liouville equations at short times matched to long-time fermionic oscillator correlators.

A shared two-Schwarzian action with a reparametrized interaction is supplemented by vanishing total SL(2) charges. Gauge reduction gives ϕ=log t′ with potential V=e^(2ϕ)−ηe^(2∆ϕ); quantization is treated exactly at ∆=1/2 and by WKB more generally.

Evaluate Euclidean disk and cut-disk saddles to obtain semiclassical Hartle–Hawking wave functions in energy and length representations. Boundary corners require different prescriptions for overlap corners, proportional to π−θ, and corners introduced by cutting states, proportional to π/2−θ.

Reduce the classical solution space modulo allowed diffeomorphisms, identify its symplectic form, transform to renormalized geodesic length and conjugate momentum, and canonically quantize an exponential-potential scattering problem. Modified Bessel functions give the energy wave functions.

Numerically solve the spherical scalar equation for NFW and Burkert halo profiles with ∂rφ(0)=0 and φ(∞)=0. Profiles are normalized to 0.3 GeV/cm³ at r=8.5 kpc; the adopted profile scales are R=20 kpc and rc=10 kpc.

Use the sourced scalar equation and, for a static approximately uniform distribution larger than relevant scales, φ≈−gXnX/mφ². Muon threshold corrections are expressed as Δα/α=(2α/3π)ln(1+Δmµ/mµ), preserving the logarithm when the mass shift is appreciable.

For cosmology, limit the effective sourcing scale by the horizon when it is smaller than the force range. Estimate φ∼−gXnXdhor², with nX∝T³, using dhor≈2/H in matter domination and 1/H in radiation domination, joined by a simple interpolation.

The desired mixed initial data are singular under naive substitution. A Laplace transform over a half-infinite q0 line replaces the delta-function structure, followed by a specified joint limit to p0=0 and Πq,0=−i. The square-root branch is chosen so that √(p0p1−N²)→+iN.

Evaluate the constant-lapse phase-space propagator directly. Linearity of the Hamiltonian in q and Πp makes these integration variables enforce classical equations, so the semiclassical propagator is exact within the truncation. Fourier transformation supplies mixed position–momentum representations.

Integrate the resulting lapse-dependent expression around a closed contour enclosing N=0. The integral may be written as a residue series; its large-volume interpretation uses steepest descent through two lower-half-plane complex saddles while avoiding the positive-imaginary-axis saddle.

Use heavy-fermion triangle loops to generate anomalous and non-anomalous gauge couplings, and chiral field redefinitions to obtain derivative spin couplings. Gauge-anomaly cancellation constrains the permitted fermion content.

Estimate cosmological abundance through misalignment and scan f, the explicit-breaking cutoff, q, N, initial angle and potential coefficient. Compare selected spin-coupling predictions with the paper's CASPEr-Wind sensitivity projections.

Identify gauge-invariant scalar operators; project scalar phases orthogonally to the eaten gauge modes and canonically normalize the remaining mode. Appendix A discretizes the fifth dimension and relates a Wilson line to the symmetry-breaking scalar product.

Review dimensional reduction, universal volume/dilaton scalings, tadpole constraints and no-scale sum-of-squares potentials. Assess candidate vacua using moduli stabilization, tachyon searches, duality frames and the assumptions of existing no-go arguments.

Review Smarr relations connecting ultraviolet energy to infrared brane charges/potentials, and integrated ten-dimensional field equations on compact manifolds. These diagnose flux singularities and the sign of four-dimensional curvature under specified source and condensate prescriptions.

Background-field expansion φ=φ0+ϕ and H=v+h, treating mS=gφ0 as locally constant over times shorter than H−1. The authors evaluate leading renormalized one-loop contributions to the scalar mass, Higgs–φ biquadratic coupling, and φ quartic; full Coleman–Weinberg resummation is mentioned but not required for their estimates.
Diagonalization of the two-neutrino mass matrix, followed by oscillation-averaged population estimates and an adiabatic extension to changing mS, including cosmological dilution factors.
Choose β through Vm=exp[−∫β dφ], giving β=−βp/φ for power potentials and β=βi/φ for inverse powers. Integrating the beta relation then supplies φ(a), with w0 setting the scalar boundary condition.

Matter continuity gives ρm=ρm0 a⁻³. An integrating-factor equation for W is converted to scale-factor integrals and incomplete Gamma functions. The full W expressions are used for w because matter-era subtraction amplifies small errors; simpler approximations are used for H.

Vary the action and reduce it to homogeneous background equations. The Bianchi identity makes only two background equations independent. For V=0, specify H(t), reconstruct ξ(t) with an integrating factor, and determine Φ(t); the nonconstant example requires numerical integration.

Iterate canonical splitting down an ordered cone, project each nilpotent, and solve polarization-preserving completion equations. The procedure requires admissible Hodge input and a specified order, beyond matrix commutativity.

Compute Deligne summands and their grading, solve the nilpotent conjugation equation, and transform the filtration. Check reality in a real basis; complex Hodge-basis entries do not themselves indicate failure.

Use nilpotent orbits to approximate periods near discriminant intersections, limiting mixed Hodge structures and Deligne splittings to classify degenerations, and the imported multivariable SL(2)-orbit theorem to construct commuting sl(2) triples recursively from the highest intersection.

The authors obtain leading-order slow-roll solutions, calculate acceleration and exit conditions, and numerically evolve the full scalaron equations beyond slow roll. KR–scalar duality is used to motivate the adopted scalar and tensor spectral formulas.

In five dimensions, integrate over the extra coordinate to obtain a radion effective action and KK modes. The analysis retains the massless KR mode and solves its wave-function equation locally near fixed-ϕ hypersurfaces by separation of variables and numerical time evolution.

An auxiliary-field formulation and conformal transformation map F(R) gravity to Einstein gravity plus a scalar potential. Four-dimensional cosmological solutions are obtained in the scalar-tensor frame and transformed back to Jordan-frame time and scale factor.

Compare order-of-magnitude axion relaxation and gravitational quantum-break times. The note uses parametric estimates rather than supplying a detailed QCD vacuum-energy function or an explicit dark-energy evolution.

Combine the historical small-ϑ bound, positive observed dark energy and an imported theorem locating the QCD energy minimum at ϑ=0. Infer higher-energy vacuum sectors and apply the adopted exclusion of quantum-breaking de Sitter vacua.

Specify a constant linear coupling, integrate the field flow and compare the predicted variation with observations. Apply the same operation separately to μ and α; equal couplings produce equal fractional tracks.

Use an integrating factor, impose W(1) = W0, then select W < 0. The operation separates the general matter-inclusive reconstruction from whether a particular potential admits a closed-form quadrature.
Approximate one generated w(a) trajectory by w0fit + wafit(1−a) over three different domains. Comparing fitted and generating behavior tests representation bias rather than physical phantom crossing.

Differentiate the input potential, integrate the resulting scalar flow and superpotential, then retain cases whose beta potential stays sufficiently close to the model shape. Matter changes the superpotential equation and requires a separate operation.

Find the field subsets satisfying each branch, compare their endpoints, and convert overlap and endpoint conditions into parameter inequalities. The paper applies this operation to the Higgs potential's decreasing slope ratio and nonmonotonic curvature ratio.

Transform the metric, combine the induced kinetic terms, integrate the canonical field map, and rescale the potential. In this application the inputs are the nonminimally coupled radial Higgs action and its symmetry-breaking quartic potential.

Transform an observational region in tensor ratio and scalar tilt into a region of normalized potential slope and curvature. The paper applies this operation to CMB constraints before projecting onto the two alternative conjecture branches.

For explicit examples, the Einstein tensor and Bianchi identity determine an anisotropic higher-dimensional stress tensor. Algebraic inequalities then test the DEC and extract the effective lower-dimensional equation of state.
The authors average the time-time Ricci component over B, use differentiated Einstein-frame conditions and a matrix trace inequality, and derive a general integrated necessary SEC inequality.
Late-time scaling ansätze S=t^η and Ω=Ω0(y)t^ξ reduce the simplified SEC inequality to an ellipse in the (η,ξ) plane, permitting analysis of acceleration and internal expansion.

The authors use GaPP to reconstruct H(z) and its derivatives with squared-exponential and Matérn nu=9/2 covariance kernels. GP hyperparameters describe correlation length and variation about the mean; kernel choice affects derivative reconstruction and uncertainty bands.

The reconstruction requires H0 and an assumed or independently supplied present matter fraction Omega0. It obtains scalar density and pressure from the background equations, uses V=(rho_phi-P_phi)/2 and dot(phi)^2=rho_phi+P_phi, and evaluates dV/dphi=(dV/dz)/(dphi/dz), with dot(phi)=-(1+z)H dphi/dz.

Bayesian evidences use MultiNest with 500 live points and tolerance 0.2, replacing the full high-multipole likelihood with its faster 'lite' version. The authors report consistency with the full-likelihood MCMC.

An effective-fluid treatment evolves the background and density/heat-flux perturbations, using the equation of state, adiabatic sound speed and rest-frame effective sound speed. Its potential-specific ingredients are drawn from earlier work.

Metropolis–Hastings MCMC uses MontePython-v3 and modified CLASS, jointly sampling cosmological and nuisance parameters. Data combine Planck TT/TE/EE and lensing, SH0ES, 6dFGS/SDSS/BOSS BAO including BOSS growth information, and Pantheon supernovae. Joint chains use R−1<0.1.

The source evolves inverse gauge couplings piecewise across specified heavy thresholds. Only the caption and prose were available; the plotted curves, axis ticks, and numerical integration were not independently inspected or reproduced.

Expand the force around the maximum, solve homogeneous constant-H evolution, propagate the displacement, and impose a final slow-roll slope tolerance. This is an application of local stability analysis rather than a newly developed general algorithm.

For a fixed supersymmetric baseline, change the ultraviolet coupling by threshold matching, count the added zero modes, insert their masses, and compare the resulting full amplitude. The paired operations prevent an inconsistent inference from the running alone.

Integrate the dimensionless scalar in ln a, using algebraic density and equation-of-state relations to remove explicit H_0 and potential normalization. Applicability requires a matter-plus-scalar background and resolution of the printed coefficient discrepancy.
Avoid very small recombination-era scalar variables by starting later, extending w as a constant to higher redshift, and comparing selected starting redshifts and dataset choices.

Replace free initial field choices by a class-specific nonlinear flow constraint, integrate each proposed history, and weight its expansion observables against correlated measurements. Resulting constraints depend on the selected initial branch, prior measure and numerical evolution.
Compare fit quality with either posterior-constrained complexity through DIC or nominal complexity through corrected AIC. Interpret rankings within a fixed dataset and likelihood convention.

Remove redundant field-origin parameters, solve the gradient constraint, and impose tracker relations where appropriate. The simplified SUGRA and DEXP formulas require their stated asymptotic regimes and are not exact for arbitrary allowed potential parameters.

Sample the constrained scalar and cosmological posterior, summarize marginal parameter intervals, and visualize selected dynamical histories. Pointwise equation-of-state percentiles illustrate behavior but do not define a simultaneous credible region for a history.

Use interior and asymptotic potential values to locate a barrier region, then solve the complete stationarity equations. The boundary comparison supplies a search guide rather than transverse equations of motion.

Construct the flux superpotential from periods, solve its Kähler-covariant supersymmetry equations, and evaluate W0. Use that solution as input for a subsequent calculation with nonperturbative Kähler dependence.

Use an uncorrected flux solution to initialize the full eight-real-field root problem, allow all fields to shift, reject kinetic-pathological candidates, and classify the resulting critical points with the physical mass matrix.
Differentiate the prepotential, assemble periods, and evaluate the Kähler pairing and flux contraction. The direct component formula is supplied, but the matrix convention is not completely expanded.

Tune racetrack coefficients jointly with the full supersymmetry equations, then test stability. The algebraic tuning relation is exact for the specified superpotential, but a calculation with frozen initial W0 is only conditional.
Convert the complex kinetic term to a real metric, form the covariant Hessian, raise one index and diagonalize. Reject indefinite metrics before assigning physical stability.

Use Wishart-form sample covariance matrices for kinetic and mass matrices. Random-matrix universality and an analogy with the multiplicative central limit theorem motivate approximately log-normal mass spectra in the cited alignment and M-theory examples.

Expand well-aligned periodic potentials to quadratic order near local minima, then diagonalize and rescale the fields into canonical coordinates. The resulting mass eigenvalues define the spectrum used in the statistical analysis.

Construct population allowance from the single-field overlap: P_al(ϑ,N_ax|M) = [∫dμ p(μ|ϑ,M) P_al(μ|N_ax=1)]^N_ax. Distribution width, central mass and population size are then scanned to obtain exclusion contours.

Use a Hubbard–Stratonovich transformation and Gaussian generating functionals to resum scalar cross-couplings. Integrating in a dimensionless scalar χ reproduces the observable correlator when its kernel satisfies K(p) = −g²/[λ²G_hh(p)].

Study small cubic and quartic one-loop corrections with a cutoff identified with M. For holographic theories, solve linearized bulk Green functions with Neumann boundary conditions and brane matching to retain the resonance tower.

Calculate heavy-fermion messenger box amplitudes, regulate them dimensionally, and match their low-energy expansion to double-trace gauge-field operators using spinor-helicity methods. Bosonic messenger contributions are expected to be similar but are not calculated.

Expand in fluctuations, apply a monomial closure, resum, and evolve the quadratic modes with their self-consistent variance. For natural inflation, the presented output suppresses the periodic force and curvature while preserving the constant Λ⁴ energy contribution.

Higher interactions are obtained by Taylor expansion. Proposed CFT tests use Witten-diagram-derived structure constants and parity-resolved OPE crossing for ⟨ΦΦaa⟩; the mixed-correlator discussion remains motivational rather than a completed structure-constant calculation.

The analysis uses the N=1 supergravity scalar potential, eliminates the small cycle through its stationarity equation, canonically normalises the volume field, differentiates the effective potential, and applies the AdS mass–dimension dictionary. The authors also report numerical diagonalisation of the full two-modulus mass problem.

Solve stationary conditions for the potential before and after confinement, and estimate Higgs-VEV shifts caused by thermal fluctuations and axion motion between periodic minima. These requirements motivate successive revisions of the parameter benchmarks.

Use a Fokker–Planck description to estimate the probability of remaining on the unstable h=0 ridge. Assuming classical slow-roll departure after a kick gives a crude exponential suppression with increasing would-be Higgs VEV.
Constrain scanning by slow roll, dominance of classical drift over quantum fluctuations, and subdominant relaxion energy during inflation. The estimates use Δa ∼ Λ_h/√g and ΔN ∼ λH_inf²/(gΛ_h²).

Reduce the cohomogeneity-one equations to ODEs with a first-order gravitational constraint. Develop local power series at a regular shrinking circle and at the O8, then use the regular series to seed numerical evolution. No analytic global solution is reported.

Obtain source matching conditions by integrating distributional equations and the F0 Bianchi identity. Analyze bubble decay channels and D8 displacement using DBI and RR couplings; the displacement calculation uses a probe approximation.

Map a classical stationary potential through its coefficient-and-field rescaling, then test whether flux and orientifold data realize the mapped coefficients. The formal mapping preserves a minimum only when it applies to the full field-dependent potential.

Compensate modulus suppression by changing allowed flux integers, then solve and differentiate each resulting potential at fixed flux. This operation distinguishes a family of large-field vacua from the asymptotics of a single fixed-flux theory.

Compute term-by-term scaling, derive necessary comparability from field equations, and test whether allowed exponents satisfy it. The operation requires fixed discrete data to be distinguished from growing flux labels and from moduli varied within a potential.

Restore the fields controlling a partial potential, verify their background-dependent EFT status, and compute full-field forces before classifying an extremum. This abstracts the paper's axion–modulus procedure while retaining its missing-metric and cutoff limitations.

Use a brane embedding function to translate a geometric separation into a superpotential prefactor. The intended tuning requires checking the induced position dynamics, stabilization and corrections in the same small-separation regime.

Evaluate canonical slopes along a candidate positive-energy path, integrate their inverse, and compare with the permitted excursion. This estimate must be supplemented by checks of transverse stability and the validity of the slow-roll reduction.

Sum dilute, widely separated instanton and anti-instanton saddles, then extract the axionic potential from the logarithm. This separates the universal combinatorics from the compactification-dependent action and prefactors.

Reviewed collider calculations include NNLO perturbative QCD, NLO electroweak corrections, parton distributions, jet methods, generators and amplitude techniques. These are reported tools supporting precision comparisons, not calculations reproduced in this review.

Reviewed nonperturbative methods include lattice-QCD calculations of hadron properties, weak matrix elements, form factors and hadronic contributions to gµ−2. Generalized parton distributions are discussed as tools for studying the nucleon's three-dimensional structure.

First solve for the axions. Use positive real moduli as input coordinates, solve for antibrane parameters and h, then filter by physical domains, V > 0, and scalar-mass signs. This maps candidate regions without directly solving the original parameter-to-modulus problem.

Substitute power laws for fields and coefficients, compare all term exponents, retain the required competitors, impose tadpole scaling, and solve the resulting equalities. Then test actual large volume and weak coupling, including e^(−φ) = τ/ρ^(3/2).

Normalize two nonzero flux magnitudes using positive a and b, solve the continuous effective theory, then transform fields and parameters back. Track the kinetic metric when discussing masses, and impose quantization and the actual O6-plane count separately.

Form the Kähler metric, its inverse, and the covariant derivatives of W while retaining X. Evaluate the supergravity F-term potential and then impose X = X̄ = 0. Setting X to zero before differentiation would discard the intended antibrane contribution.

Critical points from the inverse parametrization are filtered using V > 0, positive antibrane parameters, and mass positivity. Non-isotropic stability is then tested separately. Figure colors and qualitative shapes are known only through the supplied prose and caption.

Identify a vector within a higher-spin Stückelberg decomposition and attempt the same normalization-and-WGC procedure. The source does not supply the interaction dictionary needed to turn this outline into a general quantitative bound.
Setting the graviton interaction scale to Mp gives gm∝m/Mp; a WGC threshold g_mMp then scales as m. The source acknowledges that transferring the WGC to this setting is an unresolved step.

Fix the current's charge normalization, rescale the vector to unit current coefficient, read its kinetic coupling, and apply a magnetic-WGC tower threshold. The physical application uses the helicity-1 mode of a fundamental massive spin-2 particle.

Integrate out the heavy eigenmode on a proportional background, rewrite the answer in the light metric, and truncate by derivative order. The packet reports this operation from cited work rather than supplying its full calculation.

Bound the gradient power below and curvature above, combine them with positive a, and cancel n′/n. In this paper the cancellation works algebraically, but its curvature input does not follow from the stated assumptions as presently rendered.
Minimize ε_V across discrete geometric and flux choices, evaluate η_V, and rescale selected quantities. The rescaling freedom cannot simultaneously enforce every string-consistency requirement.

Uses the previously established bilinear potential V_F=(8κ₄²)⁻¹ρ_A Z^{AB}ρ_B, separating saxionic coefficients from shift-invariant flux–axion polynomials. Apply an imported light-dilaton equivalence-principle parametrization to estimated UV couplings. Separately diagonalize two-U(1) kinetic and mass matrices; heavy bifundamental states motivate the estimate λ≈g1g2/(12π²).

Use inverse-volume expansions and non-degenerate eigenvalue perturbation theory; expand gauge kinetic functions and matter metrics, retaining physical fermion couplings after terms proportional to the on-shell equation vanish.

Differentiate the potential in field space, establish an amplitude-dependent lower bound, evaluate each profile's maximum, and locate threshold crossings. Compare those crossings with independently determined mass turning points, fission diagnostics, and light rings.

Choose a harmonic complex phase so the metric can remain static or stationary, then numerically solve for the amplitude profile. This separates field time dependence from the time independence of the stress tensor.

Use conformal transformation and a scalar-field redefinition to work with the Einstein-frame Higgs potential, then apply warm-inflation slow-roll background equations rather than solve the full coupled evolution.
Compare r(ns) and running–tilt trajectories with published Planck confidence contours. The displayed examples fix ξ²=10^8λ, Cγ=70 and Ne=60 while varying Γ0.

Import a thermally modified curvature spectrum, including inflaton occupation and a fitted inflaton–radiation fluctuation factor G(Q), and derive tilt, tensor-to-scalar ratio and running in the author-labeled strong and weak dissipative limits.

Reinterpret the schematic cancellation (large UV value)−(large RG change)=(small IR value) by treating the IR value as input. Extend this explanatory reversal to cosmological phase transitions and final rather than initial boundary data.

Analyze fine-tuning through three qualitative criteria: a simply described emergent property, instability under fundamental perturbations, and no simple fundamental description of the special setup. Distinguish this from small fundamental parameters or simple initial conditions.

Use a qualitative effective-phase-space argument: future asymptotics select special early states, while later degrees of freedom decouple from those asymptotic constraints. No explicit boundary Hamiltonian, ensemble or entropy evolution is calculated.

Interpret the finite r=0 D1 self-energy as a tension correction. Parameterize higher-loop long-distance exchange using effective tension, effective charge and a dilaton mass; estimate the crossover maximum using the lower real branch of the Lambert W function.

Compute torus, Klein-bottle, cylinder and Möbius amplitudes; use modular transformations and Poisson resummation to relate open-string loops to closed-string exchange. Separate massless-sector cancellations from odd-winding massive exchange and extract large-radius Casimir potentials.

Generalised geometry uses E locally equal to TM ⊕ T*M. Courant brackets of generalised vielbeins define flux coefficients; nonconstant O(D,D) transformations can generate different flux backgrounds. Courant Jacobiator relations produce Bianchi identities, also obtainable from nilpotence of a twisted differential.

Buscher dualisation gauges a world-sheet global symmetry and introduces Lagrange multipliers. Eliminating the multipliers recovers the original model under the stated restrictions; algebraically eliminating nondynamical gauge fields yields the dual fields. A Wess-Zumino formulation uses H directly to handle B-field gauge subtleties.

Poisson-Lie duality replaces closed Noether currents with an on-shell Maurer-Cartan-type conservation law, allowing vector fields that are not isometries. With invariant dilaton assumed, solutions on group targets are lifted to a Drinfeld double and refactorised to obtain dual solutions.

Estimate the time needed for a stochastic displacement to reach a boundary, then approximate loss from the interval by an exponential. The hilltop application uses Hubble-time inflaton kicks and interprets boundary crossing as ending the local quantum-dominated phase.

Add stochastic forcing to a deterministic field equation, estimate random and deterministic increments over the same time interval, and compare their magnitudes. Here the interval is one Hubble time and the random increment is a horizon-scale inflaton fluctuation.

Test truncation sensitivity through quadratic curvature terms, a nonminimal scalar–curvature coupling, and alternative regulators. Numerically solve the coupled potential-sector beta functions while treating the dimensionless Planck mass as an input.

Separate transverse-traceless tensor and physical scalar fluctuations from gauge modes. Combine gauge, ghost and Jacobian contributions into a scalar-field-independent measure term; evaluate momentum integrals with a Litim-type cutoff.

Use the functional RG for the effective average action, obtain the potential flow from the regulated inverse Hessian, and differentiate its expansion around the origin to obtain coupling beta functions. Linearized stability eigenvalues determine relevance.
Matrix factorizations of ξ²−b2, with b2=s6²/4−sL sR, and their reduced tensor powers construct divisors that split on X. Differences of conjugate divisor classes give integer multiples nD−.
K3 intersection theory supplies charged hypermultiplet multiplicities, brane genera and open-string moduli; tadpole relations are then used in gravitational, mixed and pure U(1) anomaly calculations.
The Sen limit implements b2,b4,b6 scaling as ε⁰,ε¹,ε² through scalings of the model-defining sections. The leading discriminant identifies the orientifold and D7 locus ΔE=b4²−b2b6.

Use a local inertial timelike-linear-dilaton approximation behind the horizon. The argument separates the short creation scale from the curvature scale and emphasizes the dilaton's linear contribution to the Virasoro constraints.

Compare folded-string histories with relative-entropy monotonicity arguments for ANEC, and estimate gravitational time advances through Δv∼GN∫du Tuu. These comparisons motivate the proposed backreaction scenario.
Insert the classical folded-string embedding into the spacetime worldsheet stress-tensor integral, separate bulk and folding-region energy, and integrate Tuu along complete null lines.

The stability argument uses trial fluctuations, including ΠX=1/cosh(4ρ), rather than diagonalizing the Sturm–Liouville operator. For Λ<0, the background and perturbation coefficients are examined numerically in conformal gauge.

Identify physical scalar degrees of freedom in Lorentzian signature, introduce canonical momenta, and functionally integrate the nondynamical constraints before continuing the reduced perturbation action to Euclidean signature.

Use the gauge-invariant dressed axion X=ψ+[b′/(bχ′)]δχ and then its conjugate momentum ΠX. For inhomogeneous modes the momentum action has kinetic coefficient −Bn⁻¹ and potential coefficient An⁻¹; its overall sign is fixed by the gravity-decoupling limit.

Determine nonlinear onset by comparing operators on a weak-field solution. This supplies the scale outside which separated-source force estimates are meaningful, while leaving the overlapping nonlinear problem unsolved.
Use the sign of an asymptotic scattering time delay to constrain cubic vertices. This probes a different S-matrix regime from the positivity bounds discussed alongside it.

Resolve helicities before taking a mass limit, and retain the mass dependence of both interaction coefficients and currents. A small explicit coefficient does not establish a weak physical coupling when its current diverges.

Trade an equation-of-motion-type derivative interaction for mass-weighted operators using integration by parts and a perturbative field redefinition. Retain the generated interactions and separately test any claimed on-shell or charge interpretation.

Integrate out the heavy field and expand its effects at low derivatives. Interpret the resulting terms through their perturbative regime, rather than identifying a resummed truncation pole with the removed particle.

Constrain amplitudes using analyticity and unitarity, then strengthen the constraint with controlled low-energy subtraction. Treat a massless-graviton forward pole as a separate infrared obstacle rather than assuming a gapped theorem applies unchanged.

Determine EFT operators by matching low-energy amplitude coefficients after removing massless poles. Sum the allowed intermediate states instead of treating a higher-derivative operator as the fingerprint of one ultraviolet particle.

Constrain charge assignments by anomaly cancellation, invariance of neutrino-mass operators and mediator mass terms, suppression of unwanted lower-order diagrams, and absence of Majorana operators. An explicit interaction Lagrangian and scalar potential illustrate the construction.

Rotate the neutral η and ξ scalars into their mass eigenbasis and express the one-loop neutrino mass matrix through the Passarino–Veltman B0 function. A heavy-mediator approximation supplies an order-of-magnitude mass-scale estimate.
For LVS uplifting, expand around the original LVS minimum in small volume and small-cycle shifts, then provide a numerical potential illustration.
Expand the supergravity scalar potential in powers of X, integrate out heavy X, and analyze stationarity and curvature of the resulting modulus potential.

Use an O’Raifeartaigh-like sector with massive additional chiral fields. Integrating them out gives a Coleman–Weinberg correction, represented by a quartic Kähler correction that generates the X mass.

Replace diagram-by-diagram calculations by quantization in the common matter metric. Covariance fixes the potential's measure, allowing arbitrary matter interactions while retaining explicit restrictions on external fields and renormalization.

Treat the external scalar as locally constant, normalize the matter kinetic operators, compute logarithmic one-loop vacuum terms, and test factorization. The operation is restricted to matter loops and does not apply unchanged when the external scalar becomes dynamical inside a loop.

Perturb ten-dimensional supergravity around an ISD background, solve localized-source equations with Green’s functions, and evaluate the perturbed Euclidean D3 DBI action to infer the nonperturbative prefactor’s magnitude.
Expand magnetized D7 DBI and Chern–Simons actions through quadratic worldvolume flux, decompose flux into SD/ASD parts, and track orientation-dependent charge and energy contributions.

Regularize compact torus Green’s functions with the zero mode removed, express them using theta functions, and sum orbifold/orientifold images. The two-dimensional additive constant is fixed numerically by zero mean.

Compactify transverse directions on a torus and block lattice degrees of freedom into qubits to apply a one-dimensional area-law theorem. Appendix B argues equal-time clustering using positive-frequency projection, microcausality or Lieb–Robinson bounds, and Paley–Wiener analyticity.

Compare competing homologous Ryu–Takayanagi surfaces for matching boundary strips. Rewrite the entropy comparison using mutual information and vacuum entropy differences to remove UV-regulator dependence.

Relate near-horizon dimensions to charged scalar and fermion spectra. Heavy charged objects are treated through probe mean-field quantum mechanics and Born–Sommerfeld quantization, neglecting their backreaction and interactions.

A proposed 4d supergravity completion is evaluated by solving the local deformation F-terms and integrating out zi. Independently within the paper, the KS gauge-theory dictionary and infrared gaugino condensation provide a matching effective superpotential.

The authors reduce the 10d Ricci scalar to a 5d action for a radial throat-rotation profile, use a static approximation, and estimate its gradient energy. Modeling the bulk connection by one UV point accepts an O(1) error; integrating out the heavier throat phases yields the axion potential.

Estimate per-shot yields by multiplying rates by an approximate spacetime volume of field maxima, 5 × 10⁻³² m³ s, rather than performing the full locally constant field integral. Compare thermal Schwinger, purely thermal, pure-field and single-beam mechanisms.

Solve a photon Boltzmann equation for burning plasmas, including Compton scattering. Compare the resulting spectrum with thermal distributions matched to energy density, number density, low-energy behavior and the high-energy tail.

Apply cited semiclassical rates across low-, intermediate- and high-temperature instanton regimes. The imported high-temperature result requires an all-orders loop resummation using equilibrium Matsubara methods; it is not a new rate derivation in this paper.

Analytic local expansions and derivative-jump conditions are used to identify source charge and tension. The O8+ expansion reduces to the flat orientifold form as Λ→0. At O8−, a local expansion imposed with flat-space leading powers matches the numerical endpoint; this is the authors’ analytic source check.

The cohomogeneity-one ansatz reduces the bulk equations to ordinary differential equations. A perturbative series near the finite-coupling O8+ initializes numerical integration at small positive z. One initial-condition parameter is tuned so the opposite endpoint satisfies α′(z0)=0 and the required O8− conditions.

Construct many initially ingoing beams with nested phase-space scales: widths ΔLi∼ε(i)(−Λ)^(−1/2), angular-momentum ratios l/E0 of the same scale, separations ΔLi≪di≪ΔLi−1, and energies Ei∼aiΔLi. The amplitudes are subsequently tuned to produce an intermediate profile.

Use spacetime-integrated geodesic identities, Einstein constraint equations, stress-energy conservation, and integration by parts to estimate beam transport and energy exchange. Additional derivative bounds control errors beyond the low-regularity norm; Gronwall estimates enter the initial-data bounds.

Axis continuation combines angular-momentum-resolved particle-current conservation with geodesic momentum estimates. Jacobi-field equations control derivatives of transported matter; differentiated Einstein equations and induction upgrade metric and matter regularity.

Local construction uses recursive iteration and contraction estimates, followed by gluing solutions near the axis, in an intermediate region and near infinity. Renormalized equations regularize the asymptotic region; smooth compatibility controls the gluing.

Cauchy stability uses a bootstrap comparing reflected null geodesics and momenta with those of normalized, rescaled AdS. Improved flux, concentration and mass bounds close a continuity argument using the extension principle.

Use imported constant-flow solutions H=H₀e^{εN}, c_S=e^{−sN}, L_X=Ae^{s̃N}, then derive sound-speed scaling estimates and evaluate exact example potentials. Linear perturbations are reported exactly solvable within this constant-flow framework.
For monotonic scalar evolution, use a Hamilton–Jacobi description with H(φ) and three flow hierarchies associated with H, c_S and L_X.

The computational search orders charges within species, eliminates variables using the linear equations, removes common-factor and overall-sign duplicates, and rejects inconsistent partial assignments early. It tests the cubic condition only after the quadratic condition succeeds.

Diophantine analysis separates species sums from family differences. Linear equations fix Fu+ = 4FQ+ + Fν+, Fd+ = −2FQ+ − Fν+, Fe+ = −6FQ+ − Fν+ and FL+ = −3FQ+. Quadratic parametrizations and arithmetic modulo 3 and 9 constrain the remaining variables.

Flux parameters are scanned to collect classically metastable vacua and construct a normalized distribution P(Λ). Large-volume extrema and Hessian positivity constrain the allowed vacuum energy; percentile estimates are then related to the on-shell superpotential scale.

A D3-brane relative-position mode supplies φ. The authors expand its Kähler potential, solve supersymmetric stabilization for S, Ui and φ before stabilizing T, and estimate the canonically normalized scalar mass. An illustrative S-dependent superpotential couples the Higgs-like and closed-string sectors.
Keep the reference Planck scale fixed, reduce the form kinetic term, rescale to Einstein frame, and evaluate the kinetic metric on the actual spacetime-dependent scalar trajectory.
Track the complete bent five-brane embedding, rather than its circle coordinate alone. The cited M5 holomorphic-curve description supplies the qualitative geometric explanation.

Extremize only in genuinely heavy fields, expand at large effective flux, and substitute their field-dependent minima into both potential and kinetic terms. Retain the dilaton because its response occurs at the axion scale.

Isolate a common parameter, compare its lower and upper scales, and then impose background relations. In this paper the procedure eliminates |W_0| and exposes the competition between an inflationary mass target, a Kaluza–Klein cutoff and exponential volume growth.

The argument isolates the local blow-up at fixed volume, considers its shrinking-cycle limit, and then invokes Kähler-modulus independence of the prefactor to transfer the proposed χ_ax independence to the LVS regime.

The proposal tunes f(Z) to compete with period exponentials and illustrates a possible derivative-generated heavy mass. Spectator F-term compatibility and the coupled mass spectrum remain checks required for a realization.

Differentiate the correction twice along the candidate light mode, normalize by its kinetic term, and compare with the original mass. In this paper the inputs are the loop potential, winding-direction derivatives and K_{XbarX}; unspecified normalization factors remain unresolved.

Construct the primitive cross product, project the metric and harmonics onto it, and test whether freedom within the heavy plane avoids the gradient hierarchies responsible for the two-axion obstruction.
Use homogeneity and continuous coefficient freedom to eliminate flux subsets instead of solving directly for moduli. Integral-flux existence remains a separate problem.

Find the primitive integer null vector of the heavy constraints, substitute it into kinetic and instanton terms, and canonically normalize. The displayed diagonal formula applies only when kinetic mixing is absent.
Apply the F-term equations before estimating the restricted metric. This retains saxion response that a fixed fundamental decay constant multiplied by a large winding integer would miss.

Keep exponential corrections, tune the superpotential small, and use the corrected stabilization equations to soften the saxion hierarchy. The source presents this as an alternative construction with potential for both large f and a large monotonic region.

Track measure, inverse-metric and spinor-derivative powers through reduction and field substitution. Distinguish the Kähler-independent form from the volume-normalized form before comparing the gaugino interaction coefficients.

Decompose the localized source, retain its harmonic and exact components, and complete the square with that projection. Solve the bulk equation and impose periods afterward; the remaining action is a harmonic mismatch.
Determine the modular covariance of the superpotential from the Kähler transformation, represent the allowed sections through modular forms, and analyze their cusp expansions and extrema.
Test the gradient condition first, then the Hessian condition where the gradient is too small. The paper reports this procedure numerically but gives no eigenvalue tables or common fitted constants.
Sum fixed integer momentum and winding sectors, perform the worldsheet modular integral, and assemble N=1 orbifold thresholds with their subgroup weights.
Separate winding sectors to identify which whole particle tower generates the large-modulus term. Restore the perturbative logarithm to obtain a modular invariant threshold.

Add a density threshold orthogonal to the length filtration, retaining points with ρ<ρth so dense clusters appear as excised holes. An inverse nth-neighbor distance is suggested as a density estimator; the demonstration uses only two thresholds.

Reduce the filtration-ordered simplicial boundary matrix to obtain cycle birth/death times and persistence pairs. Inspect overlaps between destroying simplices to retain information discarded by persistence diagrams. JavaPlex was modified to extract these pairs.

Generally use lazy witness complexes with ν=1 and maxmin landmarks. Include an edge when some witness z satisfies max{d(l0,z),d(l1,z)}≤r+m(z), with m(z) its nearest-landmark distance; higher simplices follow from their faces.

The constraints are integrated using ξ = θk(ν)/θk[σ] and a function q with θℓ = θℓ[σ]q/ξ. The first zero of q locates the intermediate surface after gauge fixing. Generic-dimensional formulas require separate treatments for D = 3, 4 and 5, including logarithmic terms in D = 4 and 5.

Characteristic initial data reduce the Einstein equations on null sheets to Raychaudhuri, Damour–Navier–Stokes and cross-focusing constraints. Surface data comprise intrinsic curvature, null expansions and the twist one-form.
